notes: docs/plan/08-rule-catalogue.md is the specification. This file is the single source for the
analyzer's DiagnosticDescriptor, the docs/rules/ page, the `skala explain` text, the SARIF
rules[] block and the ReSharper severity mapping.
ADR-012: an id is allocated once and never re-purposed. RuleCatalogTests.RuleIds_AreAppendOnly
reads Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/allocated-ids.txt and fails the build when an id in it
is absent here or when a shipped id's `concept` changes. Retiring a rule means `retired: true`,
`scope` drives two separate things and they are not the same thing:
- Syntax | Semantic  -> whether the rule may run in --load=loose (docs/plan/07 § loose).
- Compilation        -> excluded from the per-file incremental cache, because its output for
one file depends on files the cache key does not name.
`languageVersion` is a floor and is checked against the compilation's *effective* LangVersion,
never the SDK's. A rule that suggests C# 12 syntax to a project pinned at C# 10 produces

rules.title: The file is not formatted
rules.summary: `skala format` would change this file.
rules.rationale: The formatting half of Skala and the analysis half are one report. A finding that says "this file is not formatted" carries the formatter's own edits as its fix, so a machine reading the SARIF can apply them without a second tool invocation and a human sees formatting and analysis in one list. It is a suggestion rather than a warning because formatting is unconditional and free: the gate that cares is `formatting: clean`, not a severity.

examples.bad: if(x){DoThing();}

rules.falsePositives: None by construction: the finding is produced by running the formatter, so it exists exactly when the formatter has an edit to make. A file that does not parse produces SK9010 instead and is never reported here.
configuration: Every resharper_* formatting key; the finding is whatever the configured formatter does.

rules.title: The line is over the width and nothing in it can break
rules.summary: A line exceeds `max_line_length` and the formatter had no break point to use.
rules.rationale: A 200-character string literal and a deeply-qualified generic type are not the formatter's to shorten: it never breaks a token and never breaks inside a string. Reporting it at hint makes the audit possible without making the ordinary run noisy.

examples.bad: const string Message = "…a literal 200 characters wide…";
examples.good:
const string Message =
    "…the same literal, on a continuation line…";

rules.falsePositives: None. The check is a width measurement of the formatter's own output.

rules.title: The documentation comment is not well-formed XML
rules.summary: A `///` comment does not parse as XML, so it is left exactly as written.
rules.rationale:
Malformed doc comments are common in real code — an unescaped `<`, a `
` borrowed from HTML, a tag someone forgot to close. Skala never repairs them: a formatter that repairs documentation is a formatter that changes what the documentation says. Reporting it is the whole of the response.

examples.bad: /// <summary>Returns x < y.</summary>
examples.good: /// <summary>Returns x < y.</summary>

rules.falsePositives: None known. The check is an XML parse of the comment body.

rules.title: The body style is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would change a block body to an expression body or the reverse.
rules.rationale: Body shape is cleanup rather than whitespace: changing `{ return value; }` to `=> value` rewrites syntax even when it preserves behavior. The finding is produced from the arranger's actual fixed-point edit, so `verify` and `arrange` share one implementation and one effective configuration.

examples.bad: int Value() { return 1; }
examples.good: int Value() => 1;

rules.falsePositives: None relative to the effective configuration. Formatter-off regions are excluded and every proposed tree rewrite passes the arrangement safety checks before it is reported.

rules.title: The local variable type is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would use `var` or an explicit local type under the configured preference.
rules.rationale: Whether `var` preserves the declared type is a semantic question, especially for numeric conversions, interfaces and base types. The rule binds the initializer and rewrites only when the configured direction preserves the type.

examples.bad: List<int> values = new List<int>();
examples.good: var values = new List<int>();

rules.falsePositives: None relative to the effective configuration. The rule is skipped when no trustworthy semantic model is available.

rules.title: The object creation is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would add or remove the type in an object creation expression.
rules.rationale: Target-typed `new` removes a repeated type only where the surrounding context supplies exactly that type. Binding is required so a cleanup never changes overload resolution or the constructed type.

examples.bad: List<int> values = new List<int>();
examples.good: List<int> values = new();

rules.falsePositives: None relative to the effective configuration and language version. Unresolved or differently typed constructions are left alone.

rules.title: The default value expression is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would use `default` or `default(T)` under the configured preference.
rules.rationale: A default literal is safe only when its target type is known. The semantic rule proves that target before removing a written type, and can restore the explicit form when the configuration asks for it.

examples.bad: CancellationToken token = default(CancellationToken);
examples.good: CancellationToken token = default;

rules.falsePositives: None relative to the effective configuration. Expressions without a stable target type are not rewritten.

rules.title: The null check is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would change the configured null-checking pattern.
rules.rationale: Equality operators may be overloaded, so changing `x != null` into a pattern is not merely textual. The arranger resolves the operator and runs its diagnostic-delta safety check before keeping the rewrite.

examples.bad: if (value != null) Use(value);
examples.good: if (value is not null) Use(value);

rules.falsePositives: Types whose equality operator could change the meaning are left alone.

rules.title: The empty string expression is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would use the configured empty-string spelling.
rules.rationale: The configured cleanup style chooses between the empty literal and `string.Empty`. Binding prevents a same-named member on another type from being mistaken for the framework field.

examples.bad: var text = "";
examples.good: var text = string.Empty;

rules.falsePositives: None relative to the effective configuration. Only the framework string type is recognised.

rules.title: The instance-member qualifier is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would add or remove `this.` for the referenced member kind.
rules.rationale: Adding or removing `this.` is safe only when the resulting identifier binds to the same field, property, method or event. The arranger compares symbols and reverts a rewrite that changes binding.

examples.bad: this._value = value;
examples.good: _value = value;

rules.falsePositives: Shadowed names and any rewrite that changes symbol binding are left untouched.

rules.title: The control-statement braces are not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would add or remove braces under the configured cleanup style.
rules.rationale: Brace cleanup rewrites the statement tree rather than whitespace. The rule preserves dangling-else ownership, directives, declarations and formatter-off regions before offering an edit.

examples.bad: if (ready) { Run(); }
examples.good: if (ready) Run();

rules.falsePositives: Branches whose braces carry declarations, directives, comments or control-flow meaning are retained.

rules.title: The expression parentheses are not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange --aggressive` would remove redundant parentheses.
rules.rationale: Parenthesis removal is the arranger's highest-risk syntactic cleanup and is therefore gated by `--aggressive`. It uses Roslyn precedence and refuses directive or trivia shapes whose ownership would change.

examples.bad: return (value);
examples.good: return value;

rules.falsePositives: The rule is off unless `--aggressive` is selected. Parentheses required for precedence or configured readability remain.

rules.title: The using directives are not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would sort, place or remove using directives.
rules.rationale: Sorting and placement are syntactic; removal is conservative and occurs only when the directive is unused in every loaded compilation containing the file. One id represents the fixed-point using block because the edits overlap and must be applied together.

examples.bad:
using System.Text;
using System;
examples.good:
using System;
using System.Text;

rules.falsePositives: No using is removed without semantic agreement from every owning compilation. In syntactic mode the directives are only sorted and placed.

rules.title: The predefined type spelling is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would use a keyword or framework type name under the configured preference.
rules.rationale: The declaration and member-access preferences are independent. Binding distinguishes `System.Int32` from a same-named user type before replacing it with `int`, or performs the reverse cleanup when configured.

examples.bad: Int32 value = 0;
examples.good: int value = 0;

rules.falsePositives: Only predefined framework types are rewritten; user types with similar names are ignored.

rules.title: The accessibility modifier is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would omit an accessibility modifier that matches the language default.
rules.rationale: The rule knows the language-defined default for each declaration kind and removes only an explicitly written modifier equal to it. It does not infer project API policy.

examples.bad: private int value;
examples.good: int value;

rules.falsePositives: Only modifiers identical to the C# default for that declaration are removed.

rules.title: The namespace declaration is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would use the configured file-scoped or block-scoped namespace form.
rules.rationale: Namespace form is a tree rewrite with trivia and using-directive ownership consequences. The arrangement pipeline performs it together with using placement and verifies the combined result reaches a fixed point.

examples.good:
namespace Sample;

class C { }

rules.falsePositives: Files whose directives, multiple namespaces or language version make the conversion unsafe are left unchanged.

rules.title: The trailing comma is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would add or remove a trailing comma in a supported list.
rules.rationale: A trailing comma is a token rather than whitespace, so it belongs to cleanup. The rule distinguishes single-line and multiline lists and follows their separate configuration values.
rules.falsePositives: Only list forms for which the active language version permits a trailing comma are changed.

rules.title: The static-member qualifier is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would add, remove or change a static-member type qualifier.
rules.rationale: A qualifier can be removed or replaced only if the resulting reference resolves to the same static member. The rule binds both forms and the pipeline rejects any symbol change.

examples.bad: Helpers.Create()
examples.good: Create()

rules.falsePositives: Ambiguous references and any rewrite that resolves to a different symbol are reverted.

rules.title: The argument naming style is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would add or remove argument names under the configured style.
rules.rationale: Adding a name requires the resolved parameter; removing one is safe only when the argument already occupies that parameter's position. The rule binds the selected overload and preserves names that carry ordering semantics.

examples.bad: Move(x: 1, y: 2);
examples.good: Move(1, 2);

rules.falsePositives: Unresolved calls, out-of-position arguments and expanded `params` arguments that cannot legally be named are left alone.

rules.title: The discard declaration is not arranged
rules.summary: `skala arrange` would use the configured explicit or implicit discard declaration.
rules.rationale: The cleanup preference chooses between `out _` and `out var _`. Both spell the same discard, but the change adds or removes syntax and therefore belongs to arrangement rather than formatting.

examples.bad: TryRead(out var _);
examples.good: TryRead(out _);

rules.falsePositives: Only discard designations are changed; named locals and typed non-discard declarations are preserved.

rules.title: Use a collection expression
rules.summary: A position whose type is already written out does not need the type written again in `new`.
rules.rationale: `List<string> names = new List<string> { "a" };` says `List<string>` twice, and the second one is the compiler's job. A collection expression takes its meaning from the target type, which here is the type the author already wrote. The rule is deliberately narrow because collection expressions are the opposite of the usual modernization: they have no natural type, so `[…]` is legal in some positions and not in others, and an analyzer that fires everywhere fires where it does not compile. It fires in the three positions where the type is spelled by the author and the reader can see it — a declaration with an explicit type, a `return` in a member whose return type is written, and an assignment to a plain name — and only where the created object's type is that type exactly.

examples.bad:
string[] names = new string[] { "a", "b" };
List<int> ids = new List<int> { 1, 2 };
examples.good:
string[] names = ["a", "b"];
List<int> ids = [1, 2];

rules.falsePositives: None known. The proof is one comparison: a collection expression produces an object of its *target* type and the `new` produced an object of its own, so the rule fires only where Roslyn says the two are the same. That catches every widening at once — `object[] a = new string[] { … }` is an array of `string` that throws on an `int` write and `object[] a = […]` is an array of `object` that does not; `IList<T> x = new List<T> { … }` would let the compiler pick a different implementation. Beyond that it is silent on `var`, which has no natural type to infer and gives CS9176; on any type that is not an array or `List<T>`; where the creation has constructor arguments, since `new List<T>(capacity)` records an allocation decision the rewrite loses; on dictionary-style `{ k, v }` element pairs and on object initializers; on a lambda, whose return type is inferred rather than written; and inside an expression tree. ⚠ An argument is excluded even though the parameter type is written: `M(new string[] { … })` and `M([…])` need not resolve to the same overload, because a collection expression converts to several collection types at once. ⚠ One difference is real and accepted: `List<T> x = […]` may be built with an exact capacity where `new List<T> { … }` grows, so `x.Capacity` can differ. The elements, the type and the identity do not.

rules.title: Use a file-scoped namespace
rules.summary: A file with exactly one block-scoped namespace and nothing beside it can use `namespace X;`.
rules.rationale: One level of indentation across every file in the repository, for no expressive gain. The configuration this tool serves already says `csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped`; the rule is what makes that true in code an agent wrote rather than only in code the IDE touched.

examples.good:
namespace Vixen.Core;

public sealed class Archetype;

rules.falsePositives: Only fires when the compilation unit contains exactly one namespace declaration, that namespace is the only member of the unit, it is block-scoped, it contains no nested namespace declaration, and it has no attribute lists or extern aliases after it. A file with two namespaces cannot be converted at all and is not reported; a file whose namespace declaration carries a `#if` inside its braces is skipped, because the conversion moves a brace the disabled branch may own.
rules.resharperNote: ReSharper has no inspection id for this: it drives the conversion from `csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:suggestion` and reports the result under `resharper_arrange_namespace_body_highlighting = hint`. Two mechanisms, two severities, one concept — so this rule maps to no key at all. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use a `using` declaration
rules.summary: A `using` block that runs to the end of its enclosing block is a `using` declaration.
rules.rationale: A `using` statement whose block is the rest of the scope is a level of indentation that buys nothing: the object is disposed at the closing brace either way. Written as a declaration it loses the nesting, and in a method that acquires three things it loses three levels of it. The rule fires only where the two closing braces are the same program point, because a `using` declaration disposes when its enclosing block ends and moving that point later is a behaviour change rather than a style one.
rules.falsePositives: None known. It is silent unless the `using` statement is the last statement of its enclosing block — anywhere else the object would be disposed later than it is now — and silent when the rewrite would lift a declaration into a scope where the name is already taken. That second guard scans the whole member rather than only what is in scope, because `foreach (var item in xs) { }` standing beside `using (…) { var item = 2; }` is legal today and CS0136 once the braces are gone, and a lookup at the statement cannot see it. It is also silent on `using (existingVariable)`, which has no declaration to convert, on a body that is not a block, and wherever the statement contains a preprocessor directive, since the fix deletes two braces.

rules.title: Use `is null` / `is not null` instead of `==` / `!=`
rules.summary: A null comparison written with an operator, on a type that does not define one.
rules.rationale: `x == null` calls whatever `operator ==` the type declares; `x is null` is a pattern and always tests reference (or default) equality. On a type with a user-defined `==` the two are different programs, and on a type without one they are the same program written two ways. Preferring the pattern removes the question. It also survives a later refactor that *adds* an `operator ==`, which is exactly when `== null` silently changes meaning.
rules.falsePositives: The rule is silent unless the semantic model resolves the non-null operand's type and that type declares no `operator ==`/`operator !=`, directly or on any base type. It is silent on unconstrained type parameters (where `== null` has its own lifted meaning), on `dynamic`, on pointer types, on any operand whose type could not be resolved, and inside an expression tree, where the pattern form does not compile.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ A choice, not a derivation. The author's export carries at least six inspections over this ground at four severities: merge_into_pattern (suggestion), arrange_null_checking_pattern (hint), convert_type_check_to_null_check (warning), convert_type_check_pattern_to_null_check (warning), join_null_check_with_usage (suggestion), use_null_propagation (hint). MergeIntoPattern is the closest and the mapping is recorded rather than computed. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `is T t` instead of `is T` and a cast
rules.summary: A type test whose block opens by casting the same expression to the same type is one pattern.
rules.rationale: `if (x is Widget) { var w = (Widget)x; … }` tests the type and then converts it again, and the second conversion cannot fail — the compiler emits an `isinst` and a `castclass` where one `isinst` would do. A declaration pattern is the same program with one type check, and it makes the relationship between the test and the variable something the reader no longer has to reconstruct.
rules.falsePositives: None known. It requires the cast to be the initializer of the block's *first* statement — the shape where the declaration already exists, so the fix moves one rather than inventing one — and requires the cast and the test to name the same type by symbol rather than by spelling, since `is IList` beside `(IList<int>)` share a prefix and can succeed and fail independently. An explicitly typed declaration is admitted only where its type is the tested type exactly, because a pattern variable is bound to the tested type and `object o = (Widget)x;` would not survive. It is silent on an `if` with an `else`, where the pattern variable is in scope but not definitely assigned; where lifting the name into the enclosing block would collide with another local scope of the member; and inside an expression tree, where a pattern is CS8122.

rules.title: Use `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`
rules.summary: A hand-written null guard that `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` already is.
rules.rationale: The BCL helper is one line instead of three, captures the argument expression itself through `CallerArgumentExpression` so the message cannot drift from the parameter name, and is annotated so the nullable analysis knows the argument is non-null afterwards — which the hand-written form only manages when the `throw` is the whole `if` body.

examples.good: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);

rules.falsePositives: Requires `System.ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` to exist in the compilation, so a project on an older target framework is silent rather than offered an uncompilable fix. Only fires when the guard is an `if` whose condition is exactly `x is null` or `x == null` (with the same operator-== check SK1010 makes) and whose body is exactly one `throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(x))` with no message argument and no other statement — a guard that also logs, or that throws a derived exception, or that passes a custom message, is a deliberate choice and is left alone.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_use_throw_if_null_method_highlighting = none`, so reading the key as authoritative would switch this rule off in the repository Skala was built for. That measurement is why --resharper-severities is opt-in. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `??=`
rules.rationale: The compound form says the intent once instead of naming the target twice, and it is the form that cannot drift — a rename that misses one of the two occurrences of `x` turns the long form into a silent bug.

examples.bad: _cache = _cache ?? new Dictionary<string, int>();
examples.good: _cache ??= new Dictionary<string, int>();

rules.falsePositives: Only fires when the assignment target and the left operand of the `??` are the *same* expression syntactically, and that expression is a chain of plain identifiers (`x`, `this.x`, `a.b.c`) — never an element access and never anything containing a call, because `a[i] = a[i] ?? b` evaluates the indexer twice and `a[i] ??= b` evaluates it once, which for a side-effecting indexer is a different program.

rules.title: Use a null-conditional assignment
rules.summary: An `if` whose only job is to null-check the receiver of one assignment is `?.` in C# 14.
rules.rationale: C# 14 allows a null-conditional expression on the left of an assignment, so the three-line guard around a single field or property write becomes one line that says the same thing. The rewrite is exact rather than nearly exact because the feature evaluates the right-hand side only when the receiver is non-null, which is what the `if` did.

examples.good: customer?.Order = order;

rules.falsePositives: None known. The receiver must be a chain of plain names, since the original evaluates it twice and `?.` evaluates it once. The tested expression must be the exact link of the target's chain that was guarded: `if (a.B is not null) a.B.C = v;` rewritten as `a?.B.C = v` would reinstate the NullReferenceException the guard existed to prevent, so the `?` goes where the test was. `x != null` is admitted only where the operand's type declares no `operator ==`, the same proof SK1010 makes. It is silent on an `if` with an `else`, on a body that is not exactly one simple assignment, on a compound assignment, on a receiver that is not a reference type, and inside an expression tree.

rules.title: Use `TryGetValue` or `TryAdd` instead of `ContainsKey` and a second lookup
rules.summary: `ContainsKey` followed by the indexer, or by `Add`, hashes the key twice to do one thing.
rules.rationale: `if (map.ContainsKey(key)) { var value = map[key]; … }` computes the hash, walks the bucket, throws the result away and does all of it again. `TryGetValue` does it once, and `TryAdd` is the same saving for the insert. It is filed as modernization rather than performance because it reads as a style preference and is not one: in a loop it is half the lookups, and the shorter form is also the one that cannot go stale between the two statements.
rules.falsePositives: None known, and one of the two shapes was measured wrong before it shipped. `if (!d.ContainsKey(k)) d[k] = Build();` calls `Build()` only when the key is absent; `d.TryAdd(k, Build())` calls it every time, because C# evaluates arguments before the call, and discards the result when the key was present. On Vixen that was `mesh.AddPosition(…)`, which mutates the mesh, and `edited.ToMeshData(…)`, which builds one — a behaviour change and an allocation added to the common path. So the written value must itself be a plain name or a literal, something already computed. Beyond that: two shapes only, because they are the two where the rewrite is provable — a `ContainsKey` test whose block opens by reading the same key from the same receiver, and a negated test whose whole body writes that key once. The receiver must be `Dictionary<K, V>` exactly, since `TryAdd` is not on `IDictionary<K, V>` and on a `ConcurrentDictionary` the `ContainsKey`/indexer pair is a race whose shape the rewrite would change rather than a redundancy it removes. Receiver and key must be plain names or literals, since both are evaluated once instead of twice. It is silent on an `if` with an `else`; on an explicitly typed declaration whose type is not the dictionary's value type, because `out object v` does not compile; where the name would collide with another local scope of the member; and inside an expression tree.

rules.title: Use the `Count` property, not `Count()` or `Any()`
rules.summary: `list.Count() > 0` and `list.Any()` on something that already has a `Count`.
rules.rationale: `Enumerable.Count()` has a fast path for `ICollection` and `Any()` allocates an enumerator; both are strictly more work than reading the property, and both hide from the reader that the length is already known. The value is legibility more than speed.
rules.falsePositives: Only fires when the invoked method is exactly `System.Linq.Enumerable.Count()` or `Enumerable.Any()` with no argument, the receiver's type has an accessible instance `Count` (or `Length`) property of type `int`, and the receiver expression is a plain identifier or member-access chain with no invocation in it — so `GetItems().Any()` is left alone, because reading `.Count` on it would still call `GetItems()` and the rewrite is only obviously equivalent when the receiver is a variable. Silent on `IQueryable`, where `Any()` is a database round-trip and `Count` is not the same query.
rules.resharperNote: Three inspections cover this ground: use_collection_count_property, replace_with_single_call_to_any and replace_with_single_call_to_count, all `suggestion` in the export. The first is recorded; the mapping is many-to-one from ReSharper's side. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `Enum.GetValues<T>()`
rules.summary: `Enum.GetValues(typeof(T))` returns `Array`; the generic overload returns `T[]`.
rules.rationale: The non-generic overload returns `System.Array`, so every caller casts or enumerates as `object` and boxes each member. The generic overload is typed and allocation-free per element, and it is the same call.

examples.bad:
foreach (TokenKind kind in Enum.GetValues(typeof(TokenKind))) {
}
examples.good:
foreach (var kind in Enum.GetValues<TokenKind>()) {
}

rules.falsePositives: Requires the generic `System.Enum.GetValues<T>()` to exist in the compilation, and requires the argument to be a `typeof` naming a type the semantic model resolves to an enum. A `typeof` over a type parameter, over a non-enum, or over anything the model cannot resolve is silent, and so is a call to a user-declared type that happens to be named `Enum`.

rules.title: A pure method's result is discarded
rules.summary: A bare call discards the result of a method marked System.Diagnostics.Contracts.Pure or a known immutable string transformation.
rules.rationale: Pure calls do not update their receiver. Discarding the returned string or calculation often leaves the input unchanged where a normalization or assignment was intended.

examples.bad: value.Trim();
examples.good: value = value.Trim();

rules.falsePositives: Only method-level framework PureAttribute contracts and a closed set of System.String transformations are recognized. Arbitrary methods, lookalike attributes and void calls are ignored. Assignment to a discard, storage, return and other consumption are explicit choices. Bare expression statements only; no fix can decide which value should receive the result.

rules.title: Typed equality has no matching object equality
rules.summary: A type implements `IEquatable<Self>` without overriding Equals(object).
rules.rationale: Typed and object-based consumers can otherwise disagree about equality. A class can compare equal through `IEquatable<T>` while its object equality and hash code still use identity; structs can similarly diverge from their fallback field comparison.

examples.bad: class Key : IEquatable<Key> { public bool Equals(Key? other) => other is not null; }
examples.good: class Key : IEquatable<Key> { public bool Equals(Key? other) => other is not null; public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Key key && Equals(key); public override int GetHashCode() => 0; }

rules.falsePositives: Only the framework `IEquatable<T>` with the containing type itself as T is recognized. Records and inherited object-equality overrides are accepted, and partial types report once. Types already overriding Equals(object) are left to compiler diagnostics for a missing GetHashCode. This does not prove that existing equality or hashing implementations are consistent, and no fix can infer the identity fields.

rules.title: The collection being enumerated is modified inside the loop
rules.summary: A `foreach` over a `List<T>`, `Dictionary<,>` or `HashSet<T>` whose body adds to or removes from the same collection.
rules.rationale: The BCL collections carry a version counter, and `MoveNext` throws `InvalidOperationException` the moment it sees the version move. Because the loop the rule reports has no `break`, no `return` and no `throw`, the enumerator is guaranteed to be advanced at least once after the mutation — including past the last element, where `MoveNext` still runs to return `false`. So this is not a risk that a particular input might hit: it is a throw on every execution that reaches the mutation. The standard repair is to enumerate a snapshot, which is what the fix writes.
rules.falsePositives: Four guards, and each removes a way of being wrong rather than a way of being noisy. ⚠ **The collection type is matched against a closed list of BCL types whose enumerator is version-checked** — `List<T>`, `Dictionary<,>`, `HashSet<T>`, `SortedList<,>`, `SortedDictionary<,>`, `SortedSet<T>`, `Queue<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `Collection<T>` and `ObservableCollection<T>` — never against `ICollection<T>`, because a concurrent collection is *designed* to be modified while it is enumerated and a custom implementation may be too. ⚠ **The loop expression and the mutation's receiver must resolve to the same symbol**, so `foreach (var x in a) b.Remove(x)` is not this. ⚠ **A loop body containing any `break`, `return`, `throw` or `goto` that could leave this loop is skipped entirely**, because `items.Remove(item); break;` is the one legal spelling and the rule cannot prove which of several exits a path takes. Mutations inside a nested lambda or local function are ignored for the same reason: the rule cannot say when the delegate runs. ⚠ **The fix is offered only where `System.Linq` is already in scope**, since a repair whose text does not compile is worse than no repair; and it is marked unsafe, because enumerating a snapshot is a deliberate change to what the loop iterates, not a rewrite of the same program.

rules.title: A stored delegate captures a changing loop variable
rules.summary: A delegate added to a persistent `List<TDelegate>` captures a variable declared and incremented by an enclosing for loop.
rules.rationale: Closures capture a variable rather than the value it had when the delegate was created. Delegates retained by the list can therefore all see the loop's final value instead of one value per iteration.

examples.bad: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { actions.Add(() => Use(i)); }
examples.good: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { var iteration = i; actions.Add(() => Use(iteration)); }

rules.falsePositives: The rule binds `List<T>.Add` and uses Roslyn capture analysis. It requires a delegate element type, a field receiver or a local declared outside the loop, and a control variable changed by built-in ++/-- or a nonzero constant integer +=/-= step. Other assignments and user-defined increment operators are not treated as proven changes. Per-iteration snapshots, foreach variables, nameof-only references, immediate invocations, custom Add methods and iteration-local lists are ignored. It does not infer arbitrary storage, mutation or invocation timing. A retained delegate intended to observe the final value needs an explicit suppression; no fix chooses or rewrites a captured identity.

rules.title: An enum switch omits declared members
rules.summary: A switch over a non-flags enum has neither every declared value nor a catch-all arm.
rules.rationale: A switch that silently falls through when a new enum member is added turns a closed decision into an accidental default. Listing every value makes the compiler-visible decision explicit and makes future additions show up at the switch that needs a policy.

examples.bad: return color switch { Color.Red => 1, Color.Green => 2 };
examples.good: return color switch { Color.Red => 1, Color.Green => 2, Color.Blue => 3 };

rules.falsePositives: The rule excludes `[Flags]` enums, whose combinations are intentionally open, and any switch with `default`, discard, `var` or declaration catch-all handling. It also skips pattern forms other than constants and `or` combinations rather than guessing which values a relational, negated or recursive pattern covers. Enum aliases are compared by constant value, so handling one alias handles all aliases with that value. No fix is offered because the correct behavior for a missing value is a domain decision.

rules.title: A string comparison has an implicit culture policy
rules.summary: A string.Compare overload omits a culture/comparison argument, or parameterless ToLower/ToUpper is used directly in equality.
rules.rationale: Ambient culture can change comparison outcomes across machines or requests. The correct policy may be linguistic or ordinal; spelling that policy explicitly keeps it independent of an accidental process setting.

examples.bad: return string.Compare(left, right) == 0;
examples.good: return string.Equals(left, right, StringComparison.Ordinal);

rules.falsePositives: Only bound System.String methods are inspected. Explicit CultureInfo or StringComparison overloads, invariant casing and display-oriented casing outside a direct == or != expression are ignored. The rule also accepts an explicit ignoreCase argument only when a culture is specified; a bool alone still uses ambient culture. Custom lookalikes are excluded. No fix chooses between ordinal, invariant or user-culture semantics.

rules.title: A struct uses inherited ValueType.Equals
rules.summary: A call on a concrete struct binds to System.ValueType.Equals(object) instead of a typed or overridden equality method.
rules.rationale: The inherited implementation uses object-based fallback comparison and can require boxing. Implementing a deliberate equality contract gives collections and direct comparisons a consistent typed path.

examples.bad: struct Point { public int X; } // point.Equals(other) binds to ValueType.Equals
examples.good: struct Point : IEquatable<Point> { public int X; public bool Equals(Point other) => X == other.X; public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Point point && Equals(point); public override int GetHashCode() => X; }

rules.falsePositives: The bound target must be the inherited ValueType.Equals member and the receiver must be a concrete struct. Typed overloads, overrides, records, enums, nullable values and already-boxed receivers are excluded. No fix generates equality or changes comparisons without knowing which fields define identity.

rules.title: An exception is constructed and then discarded
rules.summary: `new SomeException(...)` is an expression statement, so the exception is allocated and thrown away.
rules.rationale: Writing `new InvalidOperationException("...");` where `throw new InvalidOperationException("...");` was meant is a guard clause that does nothing. The method continues on the path the author intended to abort, and the failure surfaces later somewhere unrelated. There is no legitimate reason to construct an exception as a standalone statement: an exception object that is neither thrown, returned, assigned nor passed anywhere has no observable effect beyond its own allocation. The fix is the missing keyword.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only on an object-creation expression that *is* the whole of an expression statement, and only when the semantic model resolves the created type and that type derives from `System.Exception`. A constructed exception that is assigned, returned, passed as an argument, added to a collection or used in any other position is not an expression statement and is never seen. Construction whose constructor argument has an intentional side effect is still reported, because the exception is still discarded; that is documented rather than guarded, and no occurrence exists on either reference tree.

rules.title: An empty catch silently discards an exception
rules.summary: A filterless catch block contains no statement or explanation.
rules.rationale: An empty catch converts an exceptional path into apparent success and erases the only evidence of the failure. If ignoring an exception is deliberate, the code should say why; otherwise it should handle, log or propagate it.

examples.bad: try { Save(); } catch (IOException) { }
examples.good: try { Save(); } catch (IOException ex) { Log(ex); throw; }

rules.falsePositives: Only a truly empty, uncommented, filterless catch is reported. A comment is accepted as an explicit justification, a filter documents which exceptional condition is intentionally accepted, and any statement means the exception is not silently swallowed. No automatic fix can infer the intended recovery policy.

rules.title: `throw ex;` resets the stack trace
rules.summary: Re-throwing the caught exception by name restarts its stack trace at the `throw`.
rules.rationale: `throw ex;` inside `catch (Exception ex)` assigns a fresh stack trace to the exception, so every frame between the original throw site and this `catch` is erased. The result is a production log that points at the handler rather than at the fault, which is the one piece of information the log existed to carry. `throw;` re-throws the same exception with its trace intact. The two forms look interchangeable and are not, which is why this is worth a rule rather than a review comment.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only when the thrown expression is a bare identifier whose name is the identifier the *nearest enclosing* catch clause declares, and that name is never assigned anywhere inside the clause. Throwing a different exception, a wrapped exception, an exception belonging to an outer catch clause, a field, a parameter, or a variable the clause reassigned is not this pattern and is not reported. `throw ex;` inside a lambda, a local function or a nested catch clause within the block is excluded, because a bare `throw;` is either illegal or means something else there. ⚠ **The fix drops the catch variable's name when the rewrite leaves it with no readers**, so `catch (FormatException ex) { throw ex; }` becomes `catch (FormatException) { throw; }`. Without that second edit the repair introduces CS0168 — an unused variable — which a `fixIsSafe: true` rule may not do and which fails a build with `TreatWarningsAsErrors`. Where the clause still reads the name, in a `when` filter or before the throw, the name stays; where a clause holds two rewritable throws the deletion is carried by the last of them, so it happens once rather than twice over the same span.

rules.title: A logger message is interpolated before it is logged
rules.summary: A Microsoft.Extensions.Logging call receives an interpolated message instead of a stable message template.
rules.rationale: Interpolating before the logger sees the message eagerly renders values and discards their property names. A stable template preserves structured fields for filtering and aggregation and avoids rendering work when the log level is disabled.

examples.bad: logger.LogInformation($"Loaded {count} items");
examples.good: logger.LogInformation("Loaded {Count} items", count);

rules.falsePositives: The rule binds only calls to `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LoggerExtensions` and only the argument bound to its `message` parameter. It does not guess from method names, custom logger types or unrelated interpolated arguments. No fix is offered because choosing useful property names and preserving format/alignment semantics requires author intent.

rules.title: `async void` outside an event handler
rules.summary: An `async void` method that nothing subscribes as an event handler.
rules.rationale: An `async void` method cannot be awaited, so its caller cannot know when it finished and cannot observe its exceptions. An exception thrown after the first `await` is raised on whatever synchronization context resumed the method, which in a console or server process means an unhandled exception that terminates it. `async Task` gives the caller both. The one legitimate use is an event handler, whose delegate type returns `void` and whose exceptions the framework expects to handle, so the rule is silent there.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The rule ships disabled — `defaultSeverity: none` — and this is the interesting part of its story rather than a hedge.** It is silent on anything that could be an event handler or is bound to a delegate: an `override`, a `virtual` or `new` method (whose return type binds every override below it), any method implementing an interface member, any method whose name begins `On`, any method with the `(object, EventArgs)` shape, any method carrying an attribute, a partial method, and — the check that costs the most — every method whose name appears anywhere in the compilation in a position other than a direct invocation, which covers `+=` subscription, a method group passed as an argument and a delegate construction. That last check is why the rule is compilation-scoped and can never be served from the per-file incremental cache.

⚠ **One measurement decides the default, and it is not a finding count.** M6 stacked two reasons and docs/plan/16 § "The reference trees are a test subject" struck one of them: "the rule fires zero times on both reference trees" is a fact about those trees, never a reason to disable a rule that is right. What survives is the cost. A compilation-scoped rule's answer for one file depends on files that file's cache key does not name, so enabling it sends every run with a change down the cold path — measured at M9 over Skala's own tree with `skala check --profile`, **8.5 s against a warm 6.9 s**, with the analyzer phase going from a single tree to all of them. Charging that to every repository for a rule whose benefit is unmeasured is the trade docs/plan/08 § "Reasons that justify a cut" calls reason 2, so the rule ships off and a repository that has `async void` turns it on deliberately.

⚠ **Turning it on does not currently work the way this field used to say it did.** `IncrementalAnalysis` decides whether the warm path is available by reading `descriptor.IsEnabledByDefault`, which comes from this file and which an `.editorconfig` severity does not change — while Roslyn's driver filters on the effective severity and runs the analyzer anyway. An opted-in repository therefore keeps the warm path, and the cache drops uncacheable rule ids from what it stores, so this rule reports correctly on a cold run and silently reports nothing for unchanged files on a warm one. docs/plan/16 § "The opt-in that does not cost what it says" is the record; until it is fixed, opting in wants `--no-cache` beside it.
configuration: dotnet_diagnostic.SK3001.severity (`none` by default; set it to `warning` to enable — ⚠ the rule is compilation-scoped, so it is meant to disable the incremental cache's warm path, and until the guard reads the effective severity rather than the default it does not: pair it with `--no-cache` or expect nothing on unchanged files, docs/plan/16 § "The opt-in that does not cost what it says")
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_async_void_method_highlighting = suggestion` and this rule defaults to `none`. ReSharper's inspection fires on every `async void` including the event handlers, so a low severity is how it stays usable; this rule excludes the event-handler cases by analysis instead, and ships off for the cost reason its `falsePositives` field explains rather than for a noise reason. Reading the ReSharper key — off by default, doc 03 § "Severities" — would turn it on at suggestion.

rules.title: Blocking on an async call
rules.summary: `.Result`, `.Wait()` or `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` on a `Task` or `ValueTask`.
rules.rationale: Blocking a thread on a task is the classic ASP.NET and WPF deadlock: the continuation needs the synchronization context the blocked thread is holding, and neither side moves again. Even where it does not deadlock it consumes a pool thread for the duration, which under load is how a server stops responding to anything at all. It also re-wraps the exception in an `AggregateException`, so the `catch` a reader expects to fire does not. `await` does none of these things.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only when the receiver's type is `System.Threading.Tasks.Task`, `Task<T>`, `ValueTask` or `ValueTask<T>` as resolved by the semantic model — never on a `.Result` property of a user type that happens to be called that, and never when the type did not resolve. It is silent wherever `await` is unavailable or wrong: an entry point, a constructor, a finalizer, an operator, a property or field initializer, a `lock` body, an `unsafe` context, an expression tree, a query clause, and inside a test method, where blocking is deliberate. A fix is offered only where the enclosing method or lambda is *already* `async` and the expression is not inside a `lock`, which is where the rewrite is provably correct; elsewhere the finding is reported with no fix, because making a method `async` changes its signature and therefore its callers, which is not an edit a tool may apply unreviewed.

rules.title: A `CancellationToken` is accepted and not passed on
rules.summary: A method takes a `CancellationToken` and calls something that offers an optional one without supplying it.
rules.rationale: A cancellation token that stops at the first frame is a cancellation that does not happen. The caller sees the token accepted, assumes the operation is cancellable, and gets a request that runs to completion after the client has gone — which under load is how a server keeps working on answers nobody is waiting for. The chain has to be complete to be worth anything, and the place it breaks is always a call that offered the parameter and was not given it.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Only an *omitted optional* parameter is reported.** The called method must declare a `CancellationToken` parameter that has a default value and that this call site supplied no argument for, positionally or by name — so a method with no such parameter, an overload pair the rule would have to choose between, and a call that already passes a token are all invisible to it. A call that passes `CancellationToken.None` or `default` **explicitly** is left alone: writing the token out is how an author says the call is deliberately not cancellable, and a rule that overrides that is arguing with a decision rather than finding an omission. ⚠ **Calls inside a `catch` or a `finally` are excluded**, because cleanup that a cancellation can abort is worse than cleanup that ignores it, and that is where the exception is legitimate. Test methods are excluded for the same reason `SK3002` excludes them. The enclosing body must have exactly one `CancellationToken` in scope; with two, which one to forward is a question the rule cannot answer, so it does not ask it. The fix appends a **named** argument, which is correct whether or not the intervening optional parameters were supplied, and is marked unsafe because passing a token makes a call cancellable that previously was not — a behaviour change the author should see.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_method_supports_cancellation_highlighting = suggestion` and this rule defaults to `warning`. ReSharper's inspection fires on every call with an unsupplied `CancellationToken` parameter, including the ones this rule excludes — cleanup in a `finally`, a call that already passes `None` deliberately, a body with two tokens in scope — so a low severity is how it stays usable. This rule reaches those cases by analysis instead, and takes its band's default. Reading the ReSharper key (off by default, doc 03 § "Severities") would demote it to `suggestion`.

rules.title: A task is discarded in synchronous code
rules.summary: A task-producing invocation is used as a bare statement in a synchronous body.
rules.rationale: Discarding a task means the caller observes neither completion nor failure. An exception can surface later as an unobserved fault while the synchronous method has already reported success.

examples.bad: void Start() { SaveAsync(); }
examples.good: Task StartAsync() => SaveAsync();

rules.falsePositives: The rule reports only a bare invocation whose resolved return type derives from `Task`, inside a synchronous method, local function, lambda or constructor. Async bodies are left to compiler diagnostic CS4014. Assigning to a discard, storing, returning, awaiting or otherwise composing the task is treated as an explicit lifetime decision. No fix is offered because changing the containing API to async is a caller-wide refactor.

rules.title: A `Task` that uses a `using` resource is returned instead of awaited
rules.summary: A non-`async` method returns a task built from a `using` variable, so the resource is disposed before the task completes.
rules.rationale: Returning a task out of a `using` disposes the resource at the `return`, not when the task finishes. The task is then running against a disposed stream, connection or scope, and what the caller gets is an `ObjectDisposedException` from somewhere with no visible connection to the `using` — or, worse, a task that completes because the operation had already finished, so the bug reproduces only under load. Awaiting inside the block is the whole repair, and because the method already returns a task, adding `async` changes its signature not at all.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only where the repair is provably complete, which is a much narrower shape than the bug. ⚠ **The returned expression must name the `using` variable.** A task that does not mention the resource may still be wrong — a `using` that is a lock scope is the case — but the rule cannot prove it, and a rule that guesses about ownership is a rule that reports the correct code around it. ⚠ **Every `return` in the method is rewritten, or none is.** Adding `async` makes the method's other returns need `await` too, so the rule collects them all and withholds the finding when any of them returns something that is not a task of the method's own type — a `null`, a `default`, or a differently-typed task. ⚠ Only ordinary methods and local functions with block bodies, whose declared return type is exactly `Task`, `Task<T>`, `ValueTask` or `ValueTask<T>`, and which are not already `async`, not abstract, not partial and not iterators. Lambdas are excluded because `async` goes in a different place in each of their spellings. The fix is unsafe by declaration: an `async` method reports a synchronous throw as a faulted task rather than throwing at the call, which is a real difference for a caller that does not await immediately.

rules.title: A disposable is created in a local and never disposed
rules.summary: `var x = new SomethingDisposable();` where the local never leaves the method and is never disposed.
rules.rationale: A disposable that is never disposed holds its handle until a finalizer runs, if it has one, and for ever if it does not. The visible symptoms — a file that cannot be reopened, a connection pool that empties, a socket in `CLOSE_WAIT` — appear far from the method that leaked and under load rather than in a test. The repair is one keyword, because C# 8's `using` declaration disposes at the end of exactly the scope the local already has.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Ownership is the whole difficulty, so the rule reports only locals that provably keep it.** The declaration must be a single declarator whose initializer is literally a `new` of a type implementing `IDisposable` — never a factory method, because `Stream.Null` and `TextWriter.Synchronized` return objects the caller does not own and nothing in the call tells them apart from a fresh one, and the local must never be returned, assigned to anything, passed as an argument or a `ref`/`out`, placed in an initializer or a collection expression, captured by a lambda or a local function, or `yield`ed — every one of which is a way the object might outlive the method. It must also be *read* at least once, so that a declaration whose object is registered by its own constructor is not mistaken for a local nobody uses. ⚠ **Ownership also travels outward, through what the object hands back.** A read whose *result* is itself disposable withdraws the finding: `device = backend.OpenDevice(options)` never passes the backend anywhere and the device it produced is kept in a field, so disposing the backend at the end of the scope closes the device with it. So does a read inside a `return` expression, because `return Task.Delay(10, source.Token)` is not `return stream.ReadByte()` and nothing in the syntax tells them apart. ⚠ **A constructor argument that is itself disposable disqualifies the finding**, because `new StreamReader(stream)` takes ownership of `stream` and a `using` on the reader would close a stream the caller still owns — this is the guard that decides whether the rule is safe to apply, and it is the reason `fixIsSafe` can be true for the rest. ⚠ `Task`, `Task<T>`, `System.Threading.Timer` and `System.Timers.Timer` are excluded by name: a task is disposable and is never disposed by anyone, and a timer that is disposed at the end of the method that started it never fires. Methods that are iterators are skipped, and so is anything below C# 8, where the `using` declaration does not exist and the fix would have to re-indent a block.

rules.title: A type owns a disposable field but is not disposable
rules.summary: An instance field is constructed by its owner, but the containing type exposes no matching disposal contract.
rules.rationale: A type that constructs and retains a disposable resource owns its lifetime. If the owner cannot itself be disposed, callers have no reliable point at which to release the retained handle or asynchronously flush it.

examples.bad: sealed class Store { readonly FileStream stream = new("data", FileMode.Open); }
examples.good: sealed class Store : IDisposable { readonly FileStream stream = new("data", FileMode.Open); public void Dispose() => stream.Dispose(); }

rules.falsePositives: Ownership is inferred only from a direct object creation in an instance field initializer. Constructor-injected, factory-returned and static fields are ignored because their ownership policy is not knowable locally. A containing type that implements either disposal contract offered by the field — `IDisposable` or `IAsyncDisposable` — is accepted; it need not expose both merely because the resource does. No fix is offered because a correct implementation may need ordering, idempotence, base-class participation and additional owned fields.

rules.title: An `IAsyncDisposable` is disposed synchronously
rules.summary: A plain `using` on a type that offers `DisposeAsync`, inside a body where `await using` would compile.
rules.rationale: A type implements `IAsyncDisposable` because its cleanup does something that has to be waited for — a final flush, a graceful close, a return to a pool. Its synchronous `Dispose` therefore either blocks the thread on that work or skips it, and both are decided by the type rather than by the caller. Taking the asynchronous path is how the caller stops depending on which one this type chose.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Only where `await using` compiles, which is a narrower place than where the pattern is wrong.** The nearest enclosing method, local function or lambda must already be `async`, and the `using` must not sit in a position where `await` is illegal — a `lock` body, a constructor, an operator, an initializer, a query clause, an `unsafe` block, an expression tree. A `using` in a synchronous method is not reported at all, because making that method `async` changes its signature and is a refactor rather than an edit. ⚠ The disposed type must implement `System.IAsyncDisposable` as resolved by the semantic model, never be guessed from a `DisposeAsync` member of the right name. ⚠ **What the rule cannot know is whether this particular type's `Dispose` is a complete implementation**, and for several BCL types it is; those findings are correct and are not necessarily worth acting on, which is what a baseline entry is for rather than a reason to lower the severity. The fix inserts one keyword and is marked unsafe because `await using` introduces a suspension point where there was none, and a suspension changes when the code after it runs.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_use_await_using_highlighting = suggestion` and this rule defaults to `warning`. ReSharper treats it as a style preference; doc 08 puts the id in the disposal-and-lifetime band, where the default is `warning`, and doc 00's ninth non-negotiable says a severity comes from what the rule means rather than from how loud it is. Reading the ReSharper key (off by default, doc 03 § "Severities") would demote it to `suggestion`.

rules.title: A `Where` the next operator could have taken as its predicate
rules.summary: `xs.Where(p).First()` is `xs.First(p)`: one fewer iterator object and one fewer delegate hop per element.
rules.rationale: `Enumerable.Where` allocates an iterator that the next operator then wraps and drives, so every element crosses two `MoveNext` frames instead of one. `First`, `FirstOrDefault`, `Last`, `LastOrDefault`, `Single`, `SingleOrDefault`, `Any`, `Count` and `LongCount` each have an overload that takes the predicate directly and does the same work in one loop with no intermediate object. LINQ defines the two forms to select the same elements in the same order for the same predicate, so this is a rewrite with no semantic content — which is why it is worth a rule rather than a review comment: the longer form reads no better and costs an indirection per element.

examples.bad:
var first = items.Where(item => item.IsReady).First();
var ready = items.Where(item => item.IsReady).Count();
examples.good:
var first = items.First(item => item.IsReady);
var ready = items.Count(item => item.IsReady);

rules.falsePositives: Both calls must resolve to `System.Linq.Enumerable`. A `Where` or a `First` on `System.Linq.Queryable` is never reported, because a provider is free to translate the one-argument overload and not the predicate one; nor is a user-defined `Where`, a user-defined operator of the same name, or either call when the symbol did not resolve. The `Where` must be the `Func<T, bool>` overload: the indexed `Func<T, int, bool>` form has no counterpart on any of the consuming operators, so it is left alone. The consuming call must pass no arguments of its own and must be one of the nine operators whose predicate overload is defined to iterate identically — `Where(p).All(q)`, `Where(p).Sum(f)` and `Where(p).Select(f)` are different shapes and are not reported. A conditional access (`xs?.Where(p).First()`) is not reported, because the rewrite has to move the member binding rather than replace a name. ⚠ The one observable difference the rewrite does make is the text of the exception on an empty sequence: `Where(p).First()` throws `InvalidOperationException("Sequence contains no elements")` and `First(p)` throws `InvalidOperationException("Sequence contains no matching element")`. The type is the same and the condition is the same; a test asserting on the message string would see the change.

rules.title: Request data is concatenated into SQL
rules.summary: A value that arrived from the request is built into SQL text that a command executes.
rules.rationale: The injected text is not data to the database, it is source code. A single quote in a value ends the literal the query put it in, and everything after it is parsed as more SQL running with the application's own credentials — which is how one search box becomes `DROP TABLE` or a dump of every row the connection can see. The fix is not to escape the quote; escaping is a blocklist and blocklists are wrong at the edges, on every dialect, forever. The fix is to stop concatenating: a parameter is transmitted beside the statement rather than inside it, so the database never parses it as SQL and there is no edge case left to get wrong. Every client has the shape — `command.Parameters.Add`, Dapper's anonymous `param` object, EF Core's `FromSql($"…")` interpolated overload — and all of them are shorter than the concatenation they replace. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic because the edit is not local: introducing a parameter means changing the text, adding a binding, and choosing the parameter's type, which is three decisions rather than a substitution.

examples.bad:
var id = context.Request.Query["id"];
command.CommandText = $"select * from orders where id = {id}";

rules.falsePositives: The rule reports only a flow it can prove inside one method, from a source declared in `taint.json` to a sink declared there, with no sanitizer between them. Everything else is silence, and the exclusions are large on purpose — every one of them is a case where a report would be *wrong*, not merely unwelcome. ⚠ A method parameter is never a source. A parameter's incoming value is whatever the callers pass, which is by definition invisible from inside the method, so treating "unknown" as "suspicious" would assert a vulnerability in code that has none: a private helper ending in `command.CommandText = sql` whose callers all pass a constant with `@name` placeholders and bind properly is completely ordinary, and every report on it would be a false positive. Interpolating a *constant* is not a finding either, so `$"select … from {Schema.VersionTable}"` is silent. ⚠ `Main(string[] args)`, `Console.ReadLine`, `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable` and `File.ReadAllText` are deliberately not sources, because the principal supplying them is the principal the process runs as — there is no boundary being crossed, so there is nothing to inject. Passing a tainted value through `int.Parse` or `Guid.Parse` sanitises it, because the result is not a string. ⚠ Inter-procedural flow is out of scope (docs/plan/08), so a value that reaches the sink through a helper method is a miss rather than a report; so is a sink inside a lambda. Both are the safe direction for a rule that defaults to `error`.

rules.title: Request data reaches a process start
rules.summary: A value that arrived from the request decides which program runs, or what it is told to do.
rules.rationale: `ProcessStartInfo.Arguments` is a single string that the child process re-splits on its own rules, so a quote or an ampersand in the value is not data — it is punctuation in somebody else's grammar, and the result is a second command running as this process's user. `FileName` is worse: it chooses the program. The replacement for `Arguments` is `ArgumentList`, which passes each element to the child verbatim — exec takes an array on Unix, and on Windows .NET does the quoting itself — so there is no syntax left to escape and no shell involved. The replacement for a tainted `FileName` is a `switch` over the programs this code is allowed to run, returning the constant path for each; an allow-list is the only thing that works, because deciding whether an arbitrary path is safe to execute is not a question with an answer. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic: moving one `Arguments` string into `ArgumentList` means splitting a command line, which is exactly the parsing this rule exists to avoid guessing at.

examples.bad:
var file = context.Request.Query["file"];
Process.Start("convert", "-resize 100x100 " + file);

rules.falsePositives: The rule shares its engine and therefore its whole exclusion story with `SK5001`: a proven intra-procedural flow from a declared source only, a parameter is never a source, and unknown is never a guess. ⚠ The exclusion that matters most here is that argv is not a source, and it is a statement about where the trust boundary is rather than about finding counts. A tool that starts a program at the path its user typed is doing its job; the party supplying argv is the party the process runs as, so there is no boundary to cross and a report would be asserting a vulnerability that does not exist. ⚠ `ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList` is deliberately not a sink even when what is added to it is tainted: it is the fix this rule recommends, and reporting it would mean telling a reader that the remedy is also the disease. Argument content that the *child program* interprets — a leading `@` or `-` that some tools read as a file reference — is outside the rule, because it depends on a program Skala cannot see.

rules.title: A broken cipher, or a mode that leaks structure
rules.summary: `DES`, `TripleDES`, `RC2` or ECB mode — none of them hides a plaintext any more.
rules.rationale: `DES` has a 56-bit key, which was already marginal when it was standardised and is exhaustively searched in hours on hardware anyone can rent. `TripleDES` fixed the key length and not the 64-bit block, so a collision becomes likely after about 32 GB under one key and the plaintext starts coming back out — that is CVE-2016-2183, "Sweet32", and it is a practical attack on a long TLS connection rather than a theoretical one. `RC2` has practical key-recovery attacks. ECB is a different failure and a more visible one: it encrypts equal blocks to equal ciphertext, so the shape of the input survives encryption — the standard demonstration is a bitmap of a penguin that is still obviously a penguin afterwards. Use `Aes`, and prefer `AesGcm`, which authenticates the ciphertext as well as hiding it, so an attacker cannot flip bits in a message you will decrypt and act on. ⚠ There is no fix, and that is deliberate: swapping the algorithm compiles and changes the key length, the block size and the ciphertext format, so everything already encrypted becomes unreadable. That is a data migration, not an edit.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ The id was allocated narrower than docs/plan/08's sentence for it, and the reason is that the other half cannot be decided correctly. The catalogue wrote "weak hash/cipher (`MD5`, `SHA1`, `DES`, ECB)" and the hash half was cut — not for firing too often, which would be work for the repository rather than a defect in the rule, but because the finding would frequently be *wrong*. `MD5` and `SHA-1` have a large legitimate population in which they are not security controls at all: cache keys, ETags, content addressing, bucket selection, and every wire protocol that froze its digest choice a decade ago and specifies it normatively — an RFC 6455 WebSocket handshake is *defined* as a SHA-1 of the client key and a fixed GUID, and reporting it would assert a vulnerability in code that cannot have one. Separating that population from a password digest needs to know what the hash is compared against and what happens when it matches, which is a question about the value's use that this rule does not ask and that an intra-procedural engine could not answer if it did. ADR-012 forbids widening an id later, so the hash half needs its own number — and an argument about how it will decide the question — before it is built. What ships fires only on a type deriving from `DES`, `TripleDES` or `RC2`, and on `CipherMode.ECB` as the value assigned to a cipher's `Mode`, so `if (algorithm.Mode == CipherMode.ECB) throw` is silent: that is the guard, not the bug. A `DES` implementation kept only to decrypt an old archive is a true finding and an unwelcome one; that is what a baseline entry is for, and it is not a reason to soften the rule.

rules.title: A certificate callback that accepts everything
rules.summary: A TLS validation callback that returns `true` without looking makes the connection encrypted but unauthenticated.
rules.rationale: TLS gives you two things and they are separable: the traffic is encrypted, and the party at the other end is who the certificate says. A callback that returns `true` for every input keeps the first and throws away the second — so the connection is perfectly encrypted, to whoever answered. That is the whole content of a man-in-the-middle attack: an attacker on the path presents any certificate at all, this code accepts it, and reads and rewrites everything in both directions while both ends see a padlock. Deleting the callback restores the platform's validation, which is chain building, revocation, hostname matching and the trust store, and is years of work nobody should reimplement. If one specific self-signed certificate genuinely has to be trusted — a device on a factory network, a local development server — then pin it: compare `certificate.GetCertHashString()` against the one thumbprint you mean and return `false` for every other input. That is four lines, it is auditable, and it fails closed when the wrong certificate shows up.

examples.bad: handler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = (_, _, _, _) => true;

rules.falsePositives: Two conditions must both hold, and both are decided without following anything. The target has to be a delegate that returns `bool` and takes a `System.Net.Security.SslPolicyErrors` — which is how the rule covers `ServicePointManager.ServerCertificateValidationCallback`, `HttpClientHandler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback`, `SslClientAuthenticationOptions.RemoteCertificateValidationCallback` and the `SslStream` constructor argument without naming any of them, and how a fifth spelling arrives covered. And the value has to be provably constant-`true`: an expression body that is the literal `true`, a block whose one statement is `return true;`, or `HttpClientHandler.DangerousAcceptAnyServerCertificateValidator`. ⚠ A callback with any condition in it is silence — a thumbprint comparison, an `errors == SslPolicyErrors.None` test, a method group, a field holding a delegate. Following those is the inter-procedural analysis docs/plan/08 puts out of scope, and a wrong `error` here would fail a build over a pinning implementation. ⚠ The most common true finding is a test or a local development environment talking to a self-signed certificate, and the rule ships at `error` anyway. That is not the same situation as `SK8005`'s polling `Thread.Sleep`, which is correct code the rule cannot recognise; this is never correct code, it is an accepted risk — and an accepted risk has a way of reaching production inside a `#if` that stopped being conditional. Accept it deliberately and visibly: a baseline entry, or a `#pragma` with a justification comment. ⚠ Nothing enforces that comment today — `SK7050` is allocated in docs/plan/08 and unbuilt — so the baseline, whose diff somebody reads, is the disposal with a mechanism behind it. Not a lower severity.

rules.title: An XML reader that parses a DTD and fetches what it names
rules.summary: DTD processing plus a resolver that goes to the network or the disk is XXE.
rules.rationale: A DTD can declare an entity whose value is a URI, and a reader with a resolver will go and get it — so a document the process was merely asked to parse can read any file that process can read and reach any host it can reach, and hand the contents back inside the parsed result or out through an error message. That is XXE, and it turns an XML endpoint into a file-read and a request-forgery primitive at once. Two settings control it and either one closes the hole: `XmlResolver = null` keeps DTD parsing working for internal entities while resolving nothing external, and `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit` refuses the DTD outright, which is right when the documents are not supposed to have one. ⚠ There is no fix, because which of those two is correct depends on whether the documents legitimately carry a DTD — a question about the data, not about the code.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ The rule needs two facts where docs/plan/08's sentence named one, and the platform is why. On .NET Framework `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Parse` was enough, because the default `XmlResolver` was an `XmlUrlResolver`. On .NET Core and later the default resolver is `null`, so parsing a DTD resolves nothing external and is not XXE — a rule that fired on `DtdProcessing.Parse` alone would report, at `error` severity, every program that legitimately parses a document with entity declarations, on a platform where that is not a vulnerability. So the rule fires only where the resolver is put back *and* the DTD is parsed. Both assignments must be explicit, both must be about the same object, and both must be in the same method: a resolver assigned from a variable is silence, because whether that variable is null is a question about another method, and `XmlSecureResolver` is excluded by name because it is the mitigation. The cost of the strictness is coverage — the shape occurs zero times in either reference tree. ⚠ Known gap, stated rather than hidden: `XmlDocument` and `XmlDataDocument` have an `XmlResolver` and no `DtdProcessing`, so the two-fact rule cannot see them and they are outside it; closing that needs its own id rather than a widening of this one.

rules.title: An abstract type has a public constructor
rules.summary: Nothing outside the type hierarchy can call it, so `public` on it states something that is not true.
rules.rationale: An abstract class cannot be instantiated, so its constructor is reachable only from a derived constructor's initializer — which is exactly what `protected` allows. Written `public`, the modifier claims a caller that cannot exist, and a reader scanning the type for its public surface has to work out that this member is not part of it. `protected` says what the constructor is for. The edit is one keyword, it removes nothing any caller could have been using, and it is verified by the compiler.
rules.falsePositives: The rule is purely syntactic and fires only on a constructor declared exactly `public` inside a `class` declaration that carries the `abstract` modifier in the same file. A `protected internal`, `internal` or `private protected` constructor is left alone, because each of those is a deliberate statement about a different audience. A static constructor has no accessibility to change. Records are not reported at all: a positional record's primary constructor is a parameter list with no `ConstructorDeclarationSyntax` to edit, and a record's copy constructor has accessibility rules of its own that the compiler enforces (CS8878), so the one-keyword edit is not obviously legal there. A partial class whose `abstract` modifier sits on a different part is a miss rather than a wrong answer — the rule needs to see the modifier beside the constructor. A constructor whose `public` token carries a preprocessor directive in its trivia is skipped, because the token the fix replaces may not exist in every branch.

rules.title: An extension method extends `object`
rules.summary: The method appears in completion for every value, even though almost no extension is meaningful for every type.
rules.rationale: An extension method is an API surface projected onto its receiver type. Using `object` projects it onto every string, integer, collection, task and domain value in the program, making completion noisier and making accidental calls easy. A narrower receiver also states the contract the implementation already relies on. There is no mechanical fix: selecting that receiver is an API-design decision.

examples.bad: public static string Dump(this object value) => value.ToString()!;
examples.good: public static string Dump(this SyntaxNode value) => value.ToString();

rules.falsePositives: A deliberately universal operation can be valid, especially diagnostics and serialization helpers. The rule reports only a resolved `System.Object` receiver on a real extension method; `dynamic`, a user type named `Object`, ordinary object parameters and narrower receivers are ignored. Suppress or baseline the rare API that is intentionally universal.

rules.title: Cyclomatic complexity is over the threshold
rules.summary: The number of linearly independent paths through a member, from its control-flow graph.
rules.rationale: Cyclomatic complexity counts the decision points in a body, and it is the number that predicts how many test cases the body needs to cover. It is computed from Roslyn's `ControlFlowGraph` rather than by counting keywords, so a `switch` expression, a pattern with a `when` clause, a conditional access chain and a `&&` short-circuit are each counted the way the compiler sees them rather than the way a regular expression would. It is the least interesting of the metrics on its own — a long flat `switch` scores high and reads fine — which is why it defaults to `hint` and why cognitive complexity is the one the gate reads.

examples.bad: // a member whose control-flow graph has 40 conditional edges
examples.good: // the same logic split across members, or expressed as a table

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug.
