What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

rules.title: Cognitive complexity is over the threshold
rules.summary: How hard a member is to read, by Sonar's published definition: nesting-weighted, with no penalty for a `switch`.
rules.rationale: Cognitive complexity is the metric worth gating on, and it is the one SonarQube users actually miss. It differs from cyclomatic complexity in the two ways that matter: a `switch` over twenty cases costs one, because a reader takes it in at a glance, and a condition nested three deep costs four rather than one, because a reader has to hold three contexts to understand it. That makes it track the thing people mean by "this method is hard" rather than the thing that is easy to count. The implementation follows Sonar's specification — increments for each control-flow break, a nesting increment for each structure nested inside another, one increment per sequence of like binary operators, and increments for `goto`, recursion and each `catch` — so a number here is comparable to a number from SonarQube on the same code.
rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. The default threshold is 15, which is Sonar's own and the number doc 09's `ci` gate names.

rules.title: The member is over the statement-count threshold
rules.summary: Method length counted in statements, not in lines.
rules.rationale: Counting lines makes the metric a function of the formatter: the same body scores differently at a 100-column width and at a 160-column one, and wrapping a long argument list makes a method "longer" without changing anything a reader has to understand. Counting statements is invariant under formatting, which is the property that makes the number worth putting in a gate at all. Declarations, expression statements, and each statement nested inside a block are counted once each; a `for` header is one statement, not three.

examples.bad: // a 300-statement method
examples.good: // the same work as several members with names

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

rules.title: The type is over the member-count threshold
rules.summary: Members declared on a type, with fields counted separately.
rules.rationale: A type's member count is the crudest of the metrics and still the one that finds god objects. Fields are counted separately from methods because the two mean different things: forty fields is a data carrier, which may be exactly right, while forty methods is a type doing forty jobs. The report carries both numbers and the rule fires on the member count. A partial type is measured per declaration rather than per symbol, because that is the file a person opens.

examples.bad: // a type with 200 methods
examples.good: // the same surface split along the seams the names already suggest

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. Enum members are not counted: a 300-member enum is a table, not a god object.

rules.title: The member takes more parameters than the threshold
rules.summary: Parameter count, including a primary constructor's parameters.
rules.rationale: A long parameter list is the one design smell that is unambiguous from the outside: past about seven the call sites stop being readable and start being positional puzzles, and every one of them has to change when the list does. Primary-constructor parameters count, because they are the type's constructor whatever the syntax; doc 07 § Metrics says so explicitly.

examples.bad: void Configure(int a, int b, int c, int d, int e, int f, int g, int h) { }
examples.good: void Configure(in ConfigureOptions options) { }

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. A `this` parameter on an extension method is counted, because a caller supplies it. Generated code is excluded, which matters here: a generated `record`'s positional constructor and a DI factory's constructor are both routinely wide and neither is a design decision anybody made.

rules.title: The member nests deeper than the threshold
rules.summary: The deepest block nesting inside a member body.
rules.rationale: Nesting depth is what cognitive complexity's nesting weight is built on, reported on its own because it is the actionable half: a body six levels deep almost always has an early return or a `continue` that flattens it, and a reader can see that from the number without reading the body. A lambda body restarts the count, because a lambda is a separate reading context.
rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

rules.title: Public API without a documentation comment
rules.summary: Doc-comment coverage of the publicly visible surface, reported as a metric and — opt-in — as a finding.
rules.rationale: Comment density is the metric most likely to be gamed and the one most worth having as a *number* rather than as a finding. As an aggregate it says whether a library's public surface is documented; as a per-member warning on a repository that has never documented anything it produces thousands of findings on day one and gets switched off by lunchtime. So it ships disabled — `defaultSeverity: none` — and a repository that wants it turns it on for the paths where it means something, exactly the way doc 08 § SK1000 describes for the hot-path rules. The aggregate is computed either way and appears in the report and in `skala trend`.
rules.falsePositives: Disabled by default, so it produces nothing until a repository asks for it. When enabled it counts only members that are publicly visible through their whole containing chain, ignores accessors, explicit interface implementations, operators, finalizers, compiler-generated members, `record` positional members and anything in generated code, and treats an `<inheritdoc/>` as documentation.
configuration: dotnet_diagnostic.SK7010.severity (`none` by default; set it per path to enable)

rules.title: Duplicated block
rules.summary: A run of at least `minTokens` tokens that occurs identically, up to identifier and literal names, somewhere else in the repository.
rules.rationale: Duplication is the one SonarQube feature with no Roslyn equivalent, and the AI workflow needs it more than most: agents copy-paste by nature, and a block pasted four times is four places a fix has to land. Detection is token-level type-2 clone detection — identifiers and literals normalised to a class, keywords and punctuation kept exact — so a block copied and renamed is still found, which is the copy people actually make. A clone group is reported once, at its first occurrence, with the rest as related locations; reporting it at every occurrence would turn one problem into n findings and make the count meaningless.

examples.bad: // the same 100-token block, pasted into four files with the variables renamed
examples.good: // one method, called four times

rules.falsePositives: Not a false-positive-prone rule in the usual sense — a reported group either is or is not a token-for-token match, and the match is verified exactly rather than trusted from the rolling hash, so a hash collision cannot produce a finding. What it can do is report duplication that is deliberate. Three exclusions handle the cases that matter and are the whole of the rule's tuning: generated files are excluded from the findings and from both halves of the percentage; test files are measured but counted and reported separately, because duplication in tests is often the readable choice and gating it drives people to write worse tests; and the 100-token default is Sonar's own for C#, which is roughly 25 lines and well above the length of any idiomatic boilerplate.

rules.title: TODO or FIXME has no issue reference
rules.summary: An actionable comment has no durable place where its owner, context and completion can be tracked.
rules.rationale: A TODO in source is discovered only by someone who happens to open that line. An issue can be assigned, discussed, searched and closed; the comment remains useful as the local pointer to it. The rule accepts a URL, `#123`, or a project key such as `SKALA-123` and does not attempt to invent an issue or remove the comment.

examples.bad: // TODO: handle cancellation
examples.good: // TODO SKALA-123: handle cancellation

rules.falsePositives: Some repositories deliberately use source comments as their backlog. Those projects should disable the rule. Only TODO/FIXME markers at the start of a comment line are actionable, so prose that merely discusses those words and strings containing them are ignored. A marker carrying a URL, hash-number or conventional project issue key is accepted.

rules.title: A warning-disable pragma has no justification
rules.summary: The source suppresses one or more diagnostics without telling the next reader why the warning is wrong here.
rules.rationale: A local pragma is an explicit exception to a repository rule. Without a reason, nobody can distinguish a deliberate exception from a temporary silencing, decide whether it is still necessary, or safely remove it. The rule accepts a meaningful trailing or immediately preceding comment and never manufactures one, because a generated justification would be worse than none.

examples.bad: #pragma warning disable CA1822
examples.good: #pragma warning disable CA1822 // Called by reflection through the instance.

rules.falsePositives: A comment farther away than the immediately preceding nonblank line is not associated with the pragma. The rule checks presence and rejects blank/TODO/FIXME placeholders; it cannot prove that the prose is truthful.

rules.title: A suppression attribute has no justification
rules.summary: `SuppressMessage` or `UnconditionalSuppressMessage` omits a meaningful `Justification`.
rules.rationale: A suppression attribute survives refactoring and is easy to read past, so its reason is part of the code review record. A nonempty `Justification` tells a future reader which analyzer assumption does not hold and whether the exception can be retired. The tool reports the omission but cannot write the explanation on the author's behalf.

examples.bad: [SuppressMessage("Design", "CA1024")]
examples.good: [SuppressMessage("Design", "CA1024", Justification = "Reads the filesystem.")]

rules.falsePositives: Only attributes semantically resolved to the framework suppression types are inspected, so a user attribute with the same short name is ignored. Empty strings and TODO/FIXME/TBD/N/A placeholders are not treated as reasons; the rule cannot assess otherwise substantive-looking prose.

rules.title: `Thread.Sleep` in a test
rules.summary: A test that waits for a duration passes or fails on how loaded the machine is.
rules.rationale: A sleep encodes a guess about how long the thing under test takes. On a developer's idle laptop the guess holds; on a CI agent running sixteen jobs it does not, and the test fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the code. The failure is intermittent, so it is triaged as flakiness rather than as a defect, and a suite with a few of these stops being read at all. It also costs the sleep on every run, forever, including all the runs where the wait was not needed. What the test wants is a signal — a handle, a task, a callback, a polled predicate with a generous timeout — and every one of those is both faster and deterministic. ⚠ There is no fix: the replacement is a change to what the test synchronises on, which is a design decision and not an edit.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only where the semantic model resolves the call to `System.Threading.Thread.Sleep`, so a `Sleep` method on a user type of that name is never reported, and neither is anything at all when the symbol did not resolve. It is scoped by attribute rather than by path: the call must sit lexically inside a method carrying a recognised test attribute (`Fact`, `Theory`, `Test`, `TestCase`, `TestMethod`, `Benchmark`), which is the same set `SK3002` uses, so a sleep in a helper method a test calls, in a fixture's constructor, or anywhere in production code is outside the rule. ⚠ A `[Benchmark]` method counts as a test method for this rule because the shared helper says so; a deliberate sleep in a benchmark is the shape most likely to be reported and not wanted. The rule cannot tell a sleep that is a guess from a sleep that is the point of the test — a test of a frame limiter, a debounce, or a file watcher's coalescing window has to advance a real clock, and reports there are true and unwanted. That is what the default severity of `suggestion` and a baseline are for; a repository that wants the rule to bite promotes it in the `[**/*.Tests/**/*.cs]` section its `.editorconfig` already has.

rules.title: A skipped test has no reason
rules.summary: An xUnit `Fact` or `Theory` is disabled with an empty or placeholder `Skip` value.
rules.rationale: A skipped test is removed from the executable specification while the suite remains green. Its reason is the minimum evidence that the skip is deliberate and gives a reviewer somewhere to start when deciding whether it can be restored. No safe fix exists: the tool cannot know why the test was disabled.

examples.bad: [Fact(Skip = "TODO")]
examples.good: [Fact(Skip = "Blocked by #481: test server cannot bind IPv6 in CI.")]

rules.falsePositives: The rule resolves the attribute to `Xunit.FactAttribute` or `Xunit.TheoryAttribute`, so lookalike user attributes are ignored. A nonconstant Skip expression is also ignored because its runtime value is unknown. Empty strings and TODO/FIXME/TBD placeholders are reported; any other nonblank reason is accepted without judging its quality.

rules.title: Unknown configuration key
rules.summary: A key in the `.editorconfig` chain is not in the option registry.
rules.rationale: The Rider export carries roughly two thousand keys Skala will never implement. Reporting them at suggestion rather than warning is the difference between an audit and an uninstall.

examples.bad: resharper_cpp_indent_size = 2

rules.falsePositives: Any key outside the registry, which includes every C++, VB and XAML key in the export. That is why it is not a warning.

rules.title: The file does not parse
rules.summary: The file has parse errors, so it is reported and left byte-identical.
rules.rationale: ADR-003, and the single most important safety property in the tool: a file Skala cannot parse is a file Skala does not touch.

examples.bad: class C { void M( }
examples.good: class C { void M() { } }

rules.falsePositives: None. The check is Roslyn's own error diagnostics.

rules.title: A member's braces are split across a preprocessor branch
rules.summary: The member is emitted verbatim, because its brace structure depends on which branch is active.
rules.rationale: Roslyn parses one branch and hands back a tree describing only that one. Reindenting from it moves braces the other branch owns.
rules.falsePositives: None known; the check counts braces per branch and only fires when the branches disagree.

rules.title: The binlog is stale for this file
rules.summary: The file on disk differs from what the recorded build compiled; the current text was substituted.
rules.rationale: Analysing what the build saw rather than what is on disk would report findings against code nobody has. Substituting the current text keeps the report about the working tree and says so.
rules.falsePositives: None; it is a comparison of file content against the compilation's recorded source list.

rules.title: The binlog does not name a file that exists
rules.summary: A `.cs` file under the repository is in no recorded compilation. Rebuild.
rules.rationale: A new file that the binlog does not name is invisible to every compilation and is therefore silently unanalysed, which is the worst failure this tool can have. It is a warning and not an info for exactly that reason.
rules.falsePositives: A file genuinely excluded from compilation — a scratch file, a `.cs` under a directory with `EnableDefaultCompileItems=false` — is reported too. `skala.jsonc`'s `exclude` is the answer, and the message names the file.

rules.title: An analyzer threw
rules.summary: An analyzer raised an exception; it is disabled for the rest of the run and everything else continues.
rules.rationale: A third-party analyzer that throws on one syntax shape must not be able to turn a CI gate red for unrelated reasons — or, worse, green by aborting the run early.
rules.falsePositives: None; it reports an exception that happened.

rules.title: An analyzer package failed to load
rules.summary: A hosted analyzer package named in `skala.jsonc` could not be loaded. Never fatal.
rules.rationale: ADR-008: third-party rules are hosted, never bundled. A package that is missing, is for another framework, or drags a conflicting dependency is a configuration problem to report, not a reason to produce no report at all.
rules.falsePositives: None; it reports a load that failed.

rules.title: The formatter's output was not token-equivalent
rules.summary: A Skala bug by definition. Nothing was written and a reproduction was dropped under `.skala/crash/`.
rules.rationale: ADR-005. The check is one extra parse per file, it costs about 15 % of formatting time, and there is no flag that turns it off.
rules.falsePositives: None. A finding here is a bug in Skala.

rules.title: Use a property pattern
rules.summary: A stable reference's null guard followed by one member equality can be expressed as a property pattern.
rules.rationale: A property pattern combines the receiver's non-null requirement and a member condition. Restricting this rewrite to one member retains getter evaluation count and avoids reordering getters. Stable, non-ref, uncaptured locals and parameters avoid replacing two observable receiver reads with one.

examples.bad: bool IsReady(Item item) => item != null && item.Ready == true;
examples.good: bool IsReady(Item item) => item is { Ready: true };

rules.falsePositives: Only a non-null guard (is not null or built-in != null) and one == constant comparison are supported. The receiver must be stable local or parameter storage with no capture or ref escape. Supported member constants are integral, char, bool, enum, string and eligible null comparisons. Float, decimal, overloaded equality, conversions with different semantics, expression trees, directives and interior comments are excluded. Chained getters and multiple member tests are not consolidated.

rules.title: Use relational and logical patterns
rules.summary: Two constant-bound integral comparisons on the same stable variable can use an and/or pattern.
rules.rationale: Pattern combinators make the range being tested explicit. A safe rewrite must keep the value being tested stable, use built-in operators, and ensure each constant is representable in the input type. The rule does not assume repeated property or field reads are interchangeable.

examples.bad: bool InRange(int value) => value >= 0 && value < 10;
examples.good: bool InRange(int value) => value is >= 0 and < 10;

rules.falsePositives: Only pairs of <, <=, > or >= comparisons joined by && or || are supported, with the variable on the left of each comparison and compile-time bounds implicitly convertible to its integral/char type. Captured/ref storage, fields, properties, invocation operands, floating-point, nullable and user-defined types, expression trees, directives and interior comments are excluded. Longer chains are not flattened.

rules.title: Decode a byte span without an array copy
rules.summary: Encoding.UTF8.GetString can consume an existing byte span without a temporary ToArray allocation.
rules.rationale: Span<byte> and ReadOnlySpan<byte> already describe the contiguous bytes to decode. Calling their ToArray solely for GetString copies the bytes and allocates an intermediate array. The replacement is offered only when speculative binding selects the framework's span overload, preserving the existing span/slice computation.

examples.bad: string Decode(System.ReadOnlySpan<byte> bytes) => System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetString(bytes.Slice(1).ToArray());
examples.good: string Decode(System.ReadOnlySpan<byte> bytes) => System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetString(bytes.Slice(1));

rules.falsePositives: Only the framework Encoding.UTF8 property, GetString(byte[]) and instance Span<byte>/ReadOnlySpan<byte>.ToArray are recognized. Arbitrary Encoding implementations, LINQ ToArray, named arguments, array range rewrites and expression trees are excluded; array/null/bounds semantics are not guessed. Existing offset/count overloads are not reported. Requires an available span overload. Concurrent mutation of the input buffer is not made safe by either form; callers must synchronize it.

rules.title: Configure awaited tasks in library code
rules.summary: A bare framework Task or ValueTask is awaited where EditorConfig explicitly selects library ConfigureAwait analysis.
rules.rationale: Library code can choose not to capture its caller's synchronization context. The existing resharper_configure_await_analysis_mode policy determines whether this inspection applies; disabled, missing, invalid and UI mode do not require missing configuration. Explicit ConfigureAwait choices are respected. Scheduling policy is an author decision, so this rule reports without an automatic fix.

examples.bad:
// resharper_configure_await_analysis_mode = library
await ReadAsync();
examples.good: await ReadAsync().ConfigureAwait(false);

rules.falsePositives: Only exact framework Task, Task<T>, ValueTask and ValueTask<T> awaits are included. Derived task types and custom awaitables are excluded. Already configured awaitables, including explicit true or variable arguments, are left alone. UI mode's redundant ConfigureAwait(true) inspection is not SK3003 and is not implemented here. await foreach and await using are outside the initial scope. The prefixed configuration key wins when both spellings exist.

rules.title: File length exceeds the configured threshold
rules.summary: A file contains more physical lines than dotnet_code_quality.SK7030.threshold (default 1000).
rules.rationale: File length is a coarse review signal, not a claim that the code is incorrect. The deliberately broad 1000-line default is a configurable starting policy, not a measurement calibrated to this repository or a universal design limit. Comments, blank lines and inactive preprocessor text count. A terminal empty line after the final newline does not count; an empty file has zero lines. Splitting a file requires design judgment, so there is no automatic fix.

examples.bad: // A file with 1001 physical lines at the default threshold.
examples.good: // A file at or below its configured threshold, or an explicitly scoped higher limit.

rules.falsePositives: This is an exact physical-line measurement, not executable statement count. LF, CRLF and CR line endings have identical counting semantics. Generated files are excluded using Roslyn's normal generated-code policy. Missing, malformed, zero, negative or overflowing thresholds fall back to 1000, matching the other metrics. Only counts strictly greater than the threshold are reported. The diagnostic carries skala.metric.value.

rules.title: Use a switch expression for a returning equality chain
rules.summary: A chain of constant equality tests returning values of the same type can use a switch expression.
rules.rationale: Switch expressions express a value selected from alternatives. This rule preserves evaluation count by requiring one stable input, unique constant patterns, an explicit fallback, and identity-converted results of one type. It does not guess at numeric common-type inference, boxing, target typing or custom conversions.

examples.bad: int M(int x) { if (x == 0) return 10; else if (x == 1) return 20; else return 30; }

rules.falsePositives: Only if/else-if/else chains with at least two equality tests on one uncaptured, non-ref local/parameter are supported. Every body must contain only a value return. Integral, enum and string constant tests are supported; duplicate constants and exhaustive bool cases are excluded. Results must have identical actual and converted types across every branch. Comments, directives, custom equality, missing fallbacks, custom conversions, ref returns, caller-argument-expression capture and ambiguous pattern identifiers are excluded. Constant dependencies must be metadata constants or declared in this source file, including transitive initializers, so cached findings do not depend on another source file's body.

rules.title: Use a list pattern for guarded element checks
rules.summary: Null, fixed-length and constant element checks on an array or string can be combined into a list pattern.
rules.rationale: A list pattern states the shape being tested without repeating the receiver and indices. Requiring a stable receiver, an explicit null guard, a proven exact length, and side-effect-free built-in element comparisons keeps the rewrite local. Untested positions become discards, not slices or allocations.

examples.bad: bool M(int[]? a) => a != null && a.Length == 2 && a[0] == 1 && a[1] == 2;
examples.good: bool M(int[]? a) => a is [1, 2];

rules.falsePositives: Only one-dimensional zero-based arrays and strings of checked lengths 1 through 8 are supported, with at least one constant-index equality. The null guard must precede the length check and the element tests; a combined Length property pattern from SK1011 is also accepted. Indices must be distinct and in range, and element types/constants must have built-in integral, bool, enum or string equality. Custom indexers, floating-point values, captured/ref receivers, directives, comments, expression trees, caller-argument-expression capture and ambiguous pattern identifiers are excluded. Constant dependencies must come from metadata or this source file, including transitive initializers. Concurrent unsynchronized mutation of the input is not supported.

rules.title: Use a UTF-8 literal for constant ASCII bytes
rules.summary: Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes of a constant ASCII string can use a UTF-8 literal when passed to an existing ReadOnlySpan<byte> parameter.
rules.rationale: A UTF-8 literal avoids the temporary array allocation and runtime encoding step. The consumer must already accept a read-only byte span, and speculative binding must select exactly the same constructed method after replacement. The rule does not convert APIs that need mutable arrays.

examples.bad: void M() { Consume(System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("OK\r\n")); }
examples.good: void M() { Consume("OK\r\n"u8); }

rules.falsePositives: Only framework Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(string), constant non-null ASCII text, and direct invocation arguments bound to ReadOnlySpan<byte> parameters are supported. Byte-array or mutable-span parameters, changed overloads, user encodings, non-ASCII text, expression trees, caller-argument-expression capture, directives and interior comments are excluded. Constant dependencies must come from metadata or this source file, including transitive initializers. Embedded ASCII escapes and NUL bytes retain their values; the literal's implicit terminator is outside the span length.

rules.title: Comparison is fixed by the integral type's range
rules.summary: A relational comparison against an integral constant is always true or false over the operand type's complete range.
rules.rationale: Fixed-width integral types cannot represent values outside their declared ranges. Testing an endpoint can therefore be redundant even where the compiler does not issue CS0652. This initial rule uses exact ranges rather than treating nullable annotations as runtime guarantees. It reports without removing expressions that may throw or have side effects.

examples.bad: bool M(byte value) => value >= 0;
examples.good: bool M(byte value) => value > 0; // if zero was intended to be excluded

rules.falsePositives: Only built-in, non-lifted relational comparisons over fixed-width integral/char types and integral constants are supported. Native integers, floating point, decimal, nullable values, overloaded operators, two constant operands, and cases already reported by CS0652 are excluded. Constant dependencies must come from metadata or this source file, including transitive initializers. Flow-dependent and nullability-derived comparisons are outside this initial scope. There is no automatic fix.

rules.title: Review a self-operation on an automatic property
rules.summary: The same known automatic property is used on both sides of an assignment or built-in comparison.
rules.rationale: The compiler already reports many field/local self-operations but leaves property spellings unchecked. Arbitrary getters or setters can have deliberate behavior, so this rule requires a non-virtual source auto-property and a stable identical receiver. A report asks for review rather than deleting an operation or inventing the intended target.

examples.bad: int Value { get; set; } void M() { Value = Value; }
examples.good: int Value { get; set; } void M(int value) { Value = value; }

rules.falsePositives: Only ordinary, non-virtual, non-override, non-abstract, non-partial auto-properties declared in the same source file are supported; another file's accessor body is not a per-file cache fact. Indexers, custom accessors, ref returns, explicit interface properties, unstable receivers and compiler-covered CS1717/CS1718 cases are excluded. Comparisons are restricted to non-lifted integral/char, bool, enum and string operations; floating-point NaN tests and custom equality are not reported. No automatic fix is offered; intentional synchronization or external weaving can require suppression.

rules.title: Review explicitly unsynchronized Lazy in static state
rules.summary: A static Lazy<T> field initializer explicitly disables thread safety.
rules.rationale: Lazy<T> is thread-safe by default. Passing false or LazyThreadSafetyMode.None explicitly removes that protection; storing that instance in static state warrants review of its access policy. Adding synchronization changes factory execution and exception behavior, so there is no automatic fix.

examples.bad: static readonly Lazy<object> Cache = new(() => new object(), false);
examples.good: static readonly Lazy<object> Cache = new(() => new object());

rules.falsePositives: Only direct framework Lazy<T> constructors in static field initializers with constant false or LazyThreadSafetyMode.None are reported. Default constructors, true, PublicationOnly, ExecutionAndPublication, instance fields, ThreadStatic fields, nonconstant modes, derived or user-defined Lazy types and factory methods are excluded. Source constants must be in the same file, including transitive initializers. Static storage is a sharing risk, not proof of concurrent access: deliberate single-threaded access or external synchronization can justify suppression. Constructor assignments and static properties are outside the initial scope.

rules.title: Review LINQ in a configured hot path
rules.summary: An explicitly enabled hot-path policy reports framework Enumerable calls for cost review.
rules.rationale: There is no reliable syntactic way to identify a hot path. This rule is disabled by default; enable dotnet_diagnostic.SK4001.severity in a chosen EditorConfig path section after measuring that code. LINQ is not inherently slow, and this rule does not claim every call allocates or should be replaced.

examples.bad:
// In an explicitly configured hot path:
var result = values.Where(IsActive).ToArray();
examples.good: // Measure the pipeline and retain it, scope the policy more narrowly, or use a measured alternative.

rules.falsePositives: Only explicit method-syntax calls bound to framework System.Linq.Enumerable are included. A fluent chain produces one finding at its outermost recognized call. Empty, AsEnumerable and TryGetNonEnumeratedCount are excluded. Queryable providers, custom LINQ methods and query-comprehension syntax are outside the initial scope. This is an opt-in review policy, not an allocation counter or an automatic LINQ-to-loop rewrite. Global severity enablement applies the policy globally; per-path enablement is recommended.

rules.title: Review iteration-local delegate captures
rules.summary: A lambda or anonymous delegate in a loop body captures fresh iteration-local storage.
rules.rationale: Capturing a foreach iteration variable or a local declared in a loop body can create a closure environment for each iteration. The diagnostic identifies the capture, not a measured heap allocation count: compiler and JIT optimizations vary. A hot path may benefit from an explicit-state API, but hoisting or reusing the closure can change retained values and is not automatically safe.

examples.bad: foreach (var item in items) { callbacks.Add(() => Use(item)); }
examples.good: // If measured hot, use an API that accepts explicit state; otherwise retain the intentional captures.

rules.falsePositives: Only delegate-converted lambdas and anonymous methods directly nested in a for, foreach, while or do body are considered. Semantic capture must include a local declared in that body or the nearest ordinary foreach iteration variable in C# 5 or later. Captures of this, parameters, outside-loop locals and for initializer variables are excluded. Static/noncapturing delegates, expression trees and nested callable bodies are excluded. Foreach deconstruction variables and method-group conversions are outside the initial scope. Default hint is a review signal, not a claim that the loop is hot; promote it by path only after measuring. No fix is offered.

rules.title: Review a materialization used only by foreach
rules.summary: A framework ToList or ToArray temporary over a stable local or parameter is consumed directly by foreach.
rules.rationale: The temporary collection is not retained or indexed; it is used only to enumerate once. Removing it may save work, but can also remove an intentional snapshot and change exception timing or interactions with mutations. The rule therefore offers a review hint without an automatic fix.

examples.bad: foreach (var item in values.ToArray()) { Consume(item); }
examples.good: foreach (var item in values) { Consume(item); } // only when snapshot and timing differences are acceptable

rules.falsePositives: Only framework Enumerable.ToList/ToArray directly feeding synchronous foreach over an uncaptured, non-ref local or parameter are reported. Parentheses and static-call spelling are accepted. Query pipelines, fields, factory expressions, custom materializers, retained temporaries, awaits and yields are excluded. Any reference to the source symbol inside the loop body suppresses the hint, preserving obvious mutation/snapshot patterns including the SK2007 fix. Hidden mutation through called methods and intentional eager evaluation cannot be proved away; retain or suppress the hint when a snapshot is required.

rules.title: Use controlled assertion input
rules.summary: An xUnit assertion directly consumes a live clock, a new GUID or an unseeded random value.
rules.rationale: Live environmental input makes an assertion harder to reproduce. Prefer a controlled clock, a fixed identifier or an explicitly seeded random source where the test permits it. Real-clock and randomness-contract tests can be intentional, so the diagnostic requests review rather than inventing test data.

examples.bad: [Fact] public void Check() { Assert.Equal(expected, DateTime.UtcNow); }
examples.good: [Fact] public void Check() { Assert.Equal(expected, controlledClock.GetUtcNow()); }

rules.falsePositives: Initial coverage is xUnit: recognized Assert calls directly in semantically attributed Fact/Theory methods (including derived attributes). Framework DateTime.Now/UtcNow/Today, DateTimeOffset.Now/UtcNow, Guid.NewGuid, and Random.Shared or new Random() calls to Next/NextInt64/NextDouble/NextSingle are recognized. Seeded or unknown random instances, custom clocks/assertions, diagnostic-message arguments, nameof operands, deferred lambdas, local functions, helpers, variables carrying earlier nondeterministic values and other test frameworks are excluded. At most one finding is emitted per assertion. Deliberate clock/randomness tests may require scoped suppression. No automatic fix is offered.

rules.title: Use a field-backed property
rules.summary: A private backing field is used exclusively inside one property's get and set accessors.
rules.rationale: C# 14's field keyword preserves custom accessor logic while letting the compiler own backing storage. The fix removes the private declaration and replaces only references proven to belong to this property.

examples.bad: private int count; public int Count { get => count; set => count = System.Math.Max(0, value); }
examples.good: public int Count { get => field; set => field = System.Math.Max(0, value); }

rules.falsePositives: Only non-virtual class properties with explicit get and set bodies and a same-type private, non-readonly, non-volatile, uninitialized field are supported. Partial containing types, directives, field comments/attributes, property attributes, initializers, generic type-parameter storage, non-nullable reference storage, other consumers, other-instance accesses, nameof, ref escapes, caller-expression capture, nested functions and existing field identifiers are excluded. C# 14 is required. Both accessors must use the field; types with explicit layout or Serializable attributes are excluded. Reflection and serializers depending on the private field's name/layout are outside the proof.

rules.title: Precompute a constant character search set
rules.summary: A private static readonly character array is used only by framework span search operations.
rules.rationale: SearchValues precomputes a reusable search strategy. The fix changes existing cached storage rather than allocating SearchValues at each call, and requires available framework factory and search overloads.

examples.bad: static readonly char[] Separators = " ,;|\t".ToCharArray(); // span.IndexOfAny(Separators)
examples.good: static readonly System.Buffers.SearchValues<char> Separators = System.Buffers.SearchValues.Create(" ,;|\t");

rules.falsePositives: Initial coverage is char arrays with 4 or more distinct constant characters and at most 256 characters, used exclusively as the values argument of framework span IndexOfAny, IndexOfAnyExcept, ContainsAny or ContainsAnyExcept. Array/collection initializers and constant-string ToCharArray are supported. String.IndexOfAny, byte sets, mutable/escaping storage, partial types, directives, comments, expression trees and other-file source constants are excluded. Other static initializers and static constructors are excluded to avoid reentrant initialization differences. Requires metadata SearchValues and compatible search overloads; small sets are left alone. Measure performance for the target workload. Reflection on the private field is outside the proof.

rules.title: Freeze a private lookup-only dictionary
rules.summary: A private static readonly Dictionary with constant entries is used only for lookups.
rules.rationale: FrozenDictionary optimizes immutable lookup tables. The fix retains the original Dictionary construction and its duplicate-key checks, then freezes it. Every source reference must remain compatible with read-only lookup semantics.

examples.bad: static readonly System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int> Codes = new() { { "ok", 200 } };
examples.good: static readonly System.Collections.Frozen.FrozenDictionary<string, int> Codes = System.Collections.Frozen.FrozenDictionary.ToFrozenDictionary(new System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>() { { "ok", 200 } });

rules.falsePositives: Only private static readonly fields in non-partial classes, constructed with the parameterless framework Dictionary constructor and constant key/value collection entries, are supported. Keys must be non-nullable integral/char or string; nullable value annotations are preserved. All uses must be indexer reads, Count, ContainsKey or TryGetValue. Mutation, enumeration, Keys/Values, aliases, escapes, custom comparers, nonconstant entries, other-file constants, directives, field comments/attributes and expression trees are excluded. Requires the framework FrozenDictionary factory. Startup work increases and runtime gains require measurement. Reflection and private-field serialization are outside the proof.

rules.title: Do not mutate a copy of a readonly struct field
rules.summary: A void struct method that directly writes an instance field is called through readonly field storage.
rules.rationale: Calling a mutating struct method through a readonly field can modify a defensive copy and discard that change. The rule requires same-file evidence of a direct instance-field assignment or increment, rather than treating every non-readonly method as mutating.

examples.bad: readonly Counter counter; void M() { counter.Increment(); } // Increment directly writes Counter's instance state.
examples.good: // Choose mutable storage, an immutable replacement API, or an explicit local copy according to intent.

rules.falsePositives: The catalogue's ambiguous mutable-struct/readonly-field entry is implemented as lost mutation through readonly storage, not a ban on readonly fields inside mutable structs. Only direct readonly field receivers and non-readonly void source struct methods with a top-level assignment/increment/decrement of an instance field are supported. Constructors and init accessors of the field's declaring type, readonly members/types, read-only methods, reference types, extensions, metadata/other-file method bodies, conditional methods, expression trees, nested/conditional writes, properties and in parameters are excluded. This is report-only: removing readonly or changing an API needs author intent.

rules.title: Review a temporary params array with a span overload
rules.summary: An explicit temporary array passed to a params parameter has an accessible ReadOnlySpan overload.
rules.rationale: A span-based call may avoid the temporary array. The analyzer speculatively binds an explicit ReadOnlySpan collection expression and verifies an accessible matching overload; it does not assume two overload bodies have identical semantics.

examples.bad: Consume(new int[] { 1, 2, 3 }); // Both params int[] and ReadOnlySpan<int> overloads exist.
examples.good: Consume((System.ReadOnlySpan<int>)[1, 2, 3]); // After reviewing the overload's behavior.

rules.falsePositives: Only nonempty explicit/implicit array creations with initializers passed as the last argument to a params array parameter are reported. Requires C# 12 and an accessible same-type overload with matching preceding parameter types/ref kinds, return type and a ReadOnlySpan of the same element type. Existing arrays, empty allocations, named/omitted arguments, dynamic calls, expression trees, await elements, pointer element types and missing or inaccessible alternatives are excluded. Expanded params calls and declaration changes belong outside this initial call-site rule. Report-only because overload semantics and actual allocation elimination require review.

rules.title: Use a dedicated System.Threading.Lock
rules.summary: A private readonly object field used only by lock statements can use System.Threading.Lock.
rules.rationale: C# 13 uses the dedicated Lock API when the lock target has that type. The fix changes both the field type and its object creation, retaining the existing lock statements. It is offered only when all source references are lock targets and the framework provides the Lock API.

examples.bad: readonly object gate = new(); void M() { lock (gate) { Work(); } }
examples.good: readonly System.Threading.Lock gate = new(); void M() { lock (gate) { Work(); } }

rules.falsePositives: Only a single private readonly object field in a class, initialized directly with new object() or target-typed new(), is supported. There must be at least one lock use; every bound reference in the file, including constructed generic types, must be a direct lock target. Monitor calls, aliases, casts, escapes, reassignment, attributes, interior comments and lock bodies containing yields are excluded. Partial containing types and files with directives are excluded so references in another source file or inactive branch cannot escape the proof. C# 13 and a metadata System.Threading.Lock with the required API are mandatory. Reflection-based access to private fields is outside the proof. Shared monitors used for Wait/Pulse are never converted.

rules.title: Review exact equality of floating-point arithmetic
rules.summary: Exact equality or inequality directly compares a computed float or double arithmetic result.
rules.rationale: Binary floating-point arithmetic rounds its results. A mathematical equality can therefore differ from exact machine equality. An appropriate tolerance depends on the domain and scale; the rule reports the comparison without inventing an epsilon or replacing it with Equals.

examples.bad: bool M(double x, double y, double expected) => x + y == expected;
examples.good: // Choose a domain-appropriate comparison, or retain intentional exact equality with a scoped suppression.

rules.falsePositives: The initial scope requires a direct built-in addition, subtraction, multiplication, division or remainder operand of a built-in, non-lifted float/double == or != comparison. Plain variable comparisons, property change guards, decimal/integral arithmetic, custom operators, constant-folded comparisons, and comparisons against constant zero, NaN or infinity are excluded. Source constant dependencies must stay in the same file, including transitive initializers. It does not trace earlier arithmetic through variables or method calls. Exact floating-point contracts may be intentional and can require suppression; no automatic fix is offered.

rules.title: Review boxing despite an existing generic constraint
rules.summary: An explicit interface cast boxes a value-type-constrained type parameter before an interface method call, despite an existing matching constraint.
rules.rationale: A constrained generic call can often dispatch without boxing. An explicit cast to the already-provided interface introduces a boxing conversion. Removing it is not automatically safe: a mutating struct method may then modify the original value instead of the boxed copy, and overload selection can differ.

examples.bad: int M<T>(T value, T other) where T : struct, IComparable<T> => ((IComparable<T>)value).CompareTo(other);
examples.good: int M<T>(T value, T other) where T : struct, IComparable<T> => value.CompareTo(other); // after reviewing copy semantics

rules.falsePositives: Only explicit boxing casts immediately used as an interface method receiver are reported. The source must be a type parameter constrained to a value type and to the target interface, directly or through an inherited interface. Reference-type and unconstrained generic casts, object casts, extension methods, retained boxes, interface property access and expression trees are excluded. The rule identifies a boxing conversion, not an exact runtime allocation count; JIT optimization and deliberate copy semantics can make retaining it appropriate. No automatic fix is offered.

rules.title: Review large struct arguments in loops
rules.summary: A source struct with known field payload exceeding dotnet_code_quality.SK4007.threshold (default 64 bytes) is passed by value in a loop body.
rules.rationale: Repeated by-value calls can copy a substantial struct. This rule uses a target-independent lower bound from primitive fields and same-file nested structs, not an ABI layout guess or Marshal.SizeOf. A by-reference API may reduce copying but can change aliasing, mutation and overload behavior, so the rule is report-only.

examples.bad:
// Large has nine long fields: at least 72 bytes.
foreach (var item in items) { Consume(large); } // Consume(Large value)
examples.good: // Measure and consider a reviewed in/ref API, or retain the by-value snapshot intentionally.

rules.falsePositives: Only explicit identity-converted local/parameter arguments to by-value struct parameters in for/foreach/while/do bodies are supported. The threshold is strictly exceeded; invalid, zero or negative values fall back to 64. Size counts primitive field payload, including decimal and compiler backing fields, and recursively known same-file non-generic non-partial structs. Explicit/auto layout, other-file and metadata structs, generic structs, references, native integers, pointers, fixed buffers, ref fields and unknown fields contribute zero rather than an invented size. Layout attributes depending on another source file's constants are excluded. Padding and StructLayout.Size are ignored. in/ref/out arguments, factories, conversions, nested callable bodies and constructor calls are excluded. JIT copy elision and intentional value isolation require review. skala.size.lower_bound records the proven payload bound.

rules.title: Review commented-out statements
rules.summary: A standalone comment block parses as at least two code-like C# statements with substantial code punctuation.
rules.rationale: Disabled statements can become stale and obscure the active implementation. This is a deliberately narrow syntax heuristic: it requests review, not deletion, because a comment may be an intentional example or a record of an experiment.

examples.bad:
// Start();
// Process();
examples.good: // Explain why an example is retained, or remove obsolete code and rely on version history.

rules.falsePositives: Only standalone ordinary // groups on consecutive lines and standalone /* */ comments are examined. XML documentation, inline comments, inactive preprocessor text, strings, fenced/code-tagged examples, URLs, prose, single statements, malformed comments, incomplete parses and groups over 8192 characters or 100 line comments are excluded. A 128-opening-delimiter budget bounds parser work. The complete stripped block must parse using the file's language options and contain at least two code-like atomic statements; unsupported statement forms are skipped. No semantic binding is claimed. Unlabelled multi-statement examples can still match; add a meaningful explanation or suppress the hint. No automatic deletion is offered.

rules.title: The exception names a parameter that does not exist
rules.summary: An `ArgumentException`-family constructor is handed a `paramName` string literal that names no parameter in scope, and exactly one parameter in scope is one edit away from it.
rules.rationale: `paramName` is an ordinary string, so `throw new ArgumentNullException("vlaue")` compiles and ships. What it produces at runtime is a message, an `ArgumentException.ParamName` and a log line all naming a parameter the method does not have, which sends the reader of the failure to the wrong argument. The same slip is easier still on the rest of the family, where `paramName` is positional and sits next to the message. `nameof` is the repair: it is the same string, checked by the compiler, and it cannot go stale under a rename.
rules.falsePositives: The argument is located by the *constructor symbol's* parameter named `paramName`, never by position, so the overloads where the same slot is a message — `ArgumentException(message, innerException)`, `ArgumentNullException(message, innerException)` — are not touched, and a named argument is followed to the right slot. Only a plain string literal is examined: `nameof`, a constant, an interpolation, a variable and an empty literal are all left alone. ⚠ **The names in scope are every parameter the C# scoping rules put there**, which is deliberately more than the enclosing method: a lambda's and a local function's own parameters, an indexer's parameters, the implicit `value` of a `set`, `init`, `add` and `remove` accessor, the containing type's primary-constructor parameters, and the parameters of every enclosing function — so a nested local function that validates its caller's argument by name is correct and is not reported. The walk stops at a `static` lambda or `static` local function, whose enclosing parameters it may not name, and at the containing type, whose outer type's primary constructor is not in scope. ⚠ **A literal that resembles nothing in scope is a deliberate false negative.** The rule reports only where exactly one parameter in scope is a case-only difference or a single edit — insertion, deletion, substitution or adjacent transposition — away from the literal, and both names are at least three characters long. Where two parameters are equally close, or none is, the rule cannot say which name was meant; reporting there would be a finding whose repair `skala fix` could not write, and doc 08 ships this rule with a safe fix. A `paramName` copied from a different overload, or left behind by a rename to an unrelated word, is therefore silent rather than guessed at.

rules.title: An obsolete marker has no message
rules.summary: `Obsolete` is applied with no message, or with a placeholder message, so no caller is told what to use instead.
rules.rationale: An obsolescence is a migration instruction addressed to every caller. Without a message the compiler warning says only that something is deprecated, and the reader has to find the replacement by archaeology. This is the same requirement `SK7050` and `SK7051` make of a suppression, on the other side of the conversation: the annotation that changes what other code should do carries the reason. The tool reports the omission and never invents the replacement, because a manufactured message would be worse than none.

examples.bad:
[Obsolete]
public void Save() { }
examples.good:
[Obsolete("Use SaveAsync; this overload blocks the calling thread.")]
public void Save() { }

rules.falsePositives: Only attributes that semantically resolve to `System.ObsoleteAttribute` are inspected, so a user attribute with the same short name is ignored. The message argument is resolved against the constructor's parameter list, so the positional and `message:` spellings are one answer. A non-constant expression is accepted without inspection rather than guessed at. Empty, whitespace and TODO/FIXME/TBD/N/A placeholders are not treated as messages; the rule cannot assess whether otherwise substantive prose actually names a replacement. `DiagnosticId` and `UrlFormat` are not accepted as substitutes, because neither is shown in the compiler's warning text.

rules.title: A coverage exclusion has no justification
rules.summary: `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` omits a meaningful `Justification`, on a target framework whose attribute has the property.
rules.rationale: An exclusion changes what the coverage percentage counts, and it does so permanently and invisibly: the number goes up and nothing in the report says which code stopped being measured. The reason is the only thing that lets a later reader decide whether the exclusion is still earned. This is the third member of the family `SK7050` and `SK7051` started, and it reports the omission without writing the reason, for the same reason they do.

examples.bad:
[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]
sealed class GeneratedShim { }
examples.good:
[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage(Justification = "Thin P/Invoke shim; exercised by the integration suite.")]
sealed class GeneratedShim { }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ The rule is silent where `Justification` does not exist on the bound attribute type — it arrived in .NET 5, and demanding it of a `netstandard2.0` or `net472` compilation would be demanding something the language cannot express. The property is looked up on the symbol rather than inferred from the target framework moniker. Only attributes that semantically resolve to `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` are inspected, so a user attribute with the same short name is ignored. A `Justification` that is present and not constant-foldable counts as written. Empty, whitespace and TODO/FIXME/TBD/N/A placeholders are not reasons; the rule cannot assess whether otherwise substantive prose is true.

rules.title: A warning suppression covers nothing
rules.summary: A `#pragma warning disable` region contains no code, so it suppresses nothing and silently covers whatever is written there next.
rules.rationale: The usual way this happens is an edit: the code the pragma bracketed was deleted and the bracket stayed. What is left is a suppression waiting for a subject, and the next statement written between the directives is exempted from a diagnostic nobody chose to exempt it from. No code inside means no diagnostic inside, for every analyzer that will ever run, so the finding needs to know nothing about which analyzers those are — and the fix is to delete the directives and nothing else.

examples.bad:
#pragma warning disable CS0168
#pragma warning restore CS0168
examples.good: // Delete both directives; the code they bracketed is gone.

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ This is the decidable half of the concept and the other half is deliberately not attempted. Deciding that a suppressed warning *no longer fires* requires knowing what the compilation reports without the pragma, which an analyzer cannot ask: pragma filtering is applied to compiler diagnostics before `Compilation.GetDiagnostics` returns, an analyzer cannot enumerate the other analyzers in the run, and re-analysing from inside an analyzer is re-entrant. Only the analysis host is in a position to answer it, and doing so is a separate feature. What ships is the degenerate case: no source token between a `disable` and the `restore` that lifts it, or between a `disable` and end of file. A region holding only other `#pragma warning` directives also counts as empty, so nested empty brackets are one edit rather than several passes. Every other trivia is content and the rule stays quiet — a comment, a `#region`, and in particular inactive `#if` text, which is code under another set of preprocessor symbols. Numeric and `CS`-prefixed ids are matched as one id; a `restore` naming other ids does not close a `disable`, and a bare `restore` closes every one.

rules.title: A region is empty
rules.summary: A `#region` and its `#endregion` have only whitespace between them.
rules.rationale: A region survives every deletion inside it, so an empty one is the residue of a member that moved or went away. It is a heading over nothing, and the outline it produces claims a structure the file does not have. The fix deletes the two directive lines, which is the whole of the edit: nothing else in the file changes and no token moves.

examples.bad:
#region Serialization
#endregion
examples.good: // Delete the directives; the members they grouped are gone.

rules.falsePositives: Only whitespace counts as nothing. A comment, a `#pragma`, a `#if` and in particular inactive `#if` text are all content, and the rule stays quiet — a region that still says something to a reader is not the residue this is about, and inactive text is code under another set of preprocessor symbols. The one exception is a nested region, so that a region holding only another region is one edit rather than two `skala fix` passes. A `#region` the parser could not match to an `#endregion` is skipped, because deleting one half of an unbalanced pair would be an edit made on a guess.

rules.title: Review a goto to a label
rules.summary: A `goto` names a label, so control leaves the statement nesting. `goto case` and `goto default` are not reported.
rules.rationale: ⚠ The position, because `goto` is legal and occasionally right. `goto case` and `goto default` are the only way C# expresses switch fall-through, they cannot leave the switch they are written in, and the flow they describe is already in front of the reader — reporting them would make this a style opinion about `switch` and get the whole rule turned off. A `goto` to a label is the other thing: its target is anywhere in the enclosing member, so what runs next can no longer be read off the nesting. Neither can it be computed: `SK7001` and `SK7002` derive complexity from the structure of the statements, and a label jump is an edge those numbers do not contain, which is why the rule sits in the same range as the metrics it distorts.

examples.good: // Extract the search, return early, or use a flag — whichever says what the loop means.

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ Report-only, and this is one of the two rules the catalogue's shipping bar allows no fix for. Breaking out of nested loops is a real use with no mechanical rewrite: a flag, an extracted method and an early return are all correct and choosing between them is a design decision about what the loop means, so an edit that guessed would be worse than the `goto`. Every `goto` to a label is reported, including one inside a `switch` section, because the label is not confined to the switch. `goto case` and `goto default` are never reported. Generated code is excluded, which is where nearly all remaining `goto` lives — parser and state-machine generators emit it by design.

rules.title: Detect NaN with IsNaN rather than equality
rules.summary: A floating-point value is compared with == or != against a constant NaN, which is the one comparison guaranteed never to answer the question it was written to ask.
rules.rationale: NaN is unordered with everything including itself, so `x == double.NaN` is false even when x is NaN and `x != double.NaN` is true even when it is. The check written to catch the bad case is the shape that cannot catch it. `double.IsNaN` is the operation that was meant, and the rewrite is mechanical.

examples.bad: if (result == double.NaN) { Report(); }
examples.good: if (double.IsNaN(result)) { Report(); }

rules.falsePositives: Only `==` and `!=` between two floating-point operands are examined, and exactly one side must be a compile-time constant NaN: `double.NaN`, `float.NaN`, a `const` initialized from one, or a constant expression that folds to NaN. `!=` is reported alongside `==` because it is always true rather than always false; it carries its own message and a negated fix. NaN reached through a non-constant field, property, method result or parameter is one indirection the rule does not follow, because a `static readonly double` is not decidable from the comparison alone. Lifted comparisons on nullable operands, user-defined equality operators, operands whose own type is not `float` or `double` before conversion, and comparisons with NaN on both sides are excluded; the last names no operand to test. Relational comparisons with NaN are also constant and are deliberately not reported, because the rewrite is not a single `IsNaN` call. SK2003 excludes NaN sentinels, so the two rules do not overlap.

rules.title: Do not discard a setter's value parameter
rules.summary: A property, indexer or init accessor body does work and never mentions `value`, so every assignment through it is discarded while appearing to succeed.
rules.rationale: The setter's whole contract is to consume `value`. One that runs statements and never reads it stores something else, or stores nothing, and the caller has no way to see that the write went nowhere. The repair is a decision about what the setter was meant to store, so the rule reports and does not rewrite.

examples.bad: public int Retries { get => retries; set => retries = DefaultRetries; }
examples.good: public int Retries { get => retries; set => retries = value; }

rules.falsePositives: Only accessors with a body are examined; auto-properties, abstract, extern, interface and partial declarations have none. Three shapes earn an exemption because the discard is legible as deliberate rather than accidental: a body with no statements at all (`set { }`), a body that only throws, and an accessor or member carrying `[Obsolete]`. That is the line: an empty setter announces that it ignores the write, and a setter that does work while ignoring it does not. `value` counts as read wherever it is mentioned in the body, including inside a lambda, a local function, a nested accessor and `nameof(value)` — the last is conservative on purpose, since a name mentioned is a name the author had in mind. Statements the file's preprocessor directives disable are not in the body, so a setter emptied by `#if` reads as the empty exemption. The rule does not judge whether the value stored is the right one, only whether one was read.

rules.title: Remove GC.SuppressFinalize from a type with no finalizer
rules.summary: `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` is called from a sealed class that declares no finalizer and derives directly from object, so there is no finalizer anywhere to suppress.
rules.rationale: The call is copied out of the canonical Dispose pattern into types that never had a finalizer. It costs nothing at runtime and reads as though the type has one, which sends the next reader looking for a finalizer that is not there. Deleting the statement is the whole repair.
rules.falsePositives: Reported only for `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` written as a statement directly inside a block, in a sealed class that derives straight from object and declares no finalizer in a single non-partial declaration. Every part of that is load-bearing. ⚠ An unsealed type is excluded because a derived type may declare a finalizer, which makes the base's call the thing that suppresses it; a type with any base class other than object is excluded for the same reason one level up. A partial or multi-file declaration is excluded so the answer stays decidable from the file the finding is in, which is what `scope: Semantic` promises the cache. Structs are excluded: they cannot have finalizers at all, so the call is redundant there too, but it also boxes and that is a different finding. An argument that is not literally `this`, a call in an expression-bodied member, and a call as an embedded statement under an `if` are all excluded, because the fix is a deletion and each of those has no statement to delete or leaves a construct behind that does not compile. Reflection or a runtime-registered finalizer is outside the proof.
rules.resharperNote: The export sets `resharper_gc_suppress_finalize_for_type_without_destructor_highlighting` to `warning` and Skala defaults the rule to `suggestion`, so `--resharper-severities` raises it. The lower default is deliberate: the call is harmless at runtime, so this is source noise rather than a defect, and a gate that fails on it would fail on tidiness.

rules.title: Do not stackalloc inside a loop
rules.summary: A `stackalloc` sits in a loop body, condition or incrementor, so the frame grows by one buffer per iteration and none of them is released until the method returns.
rules.rationale: Stack memory allocated in a method is reclaimed when that method returns, not when the block ends. A `stackalloc` a loop repeats therefore grows the frame by an amount the loop bound decides, and the overflow it eventually causes is a process kill with no catchable exception and no diagnostic naming this line. No fix is offered: hoisting the buffer out of the loop changes its lifetime and whether iterations share it, which is a decision about the program rather than a rewrite of it.
rules.falsePositives: Purely syntactic: the enclosing `for`, `foreach`, `while` or `do` is found by walking outward and stopping at a lambda, an anonymous method, a local function or a member body, because a separate frame releases its own stack on return. Positions a loop evaluates only once are excluded — a `for` initializer or declaration, and a `foreach` source expression — while conditions and incrementors are reported, since a loop re-evaluates those. ⚠ A loop that cannot reach a second iteration is excluded and this is the judgement the rule makes deliberately: `do { … } while (false)`, `while (false)`, and a body whose direct statements include an unconditional `break`, `return` or `throw`. That last exclusion is withdrawn when the body contains a `continue` or a `goto` of its own, because either can reach the `stackalloc` again and the `break` then proves nothing. Conditional exits, loop bounds and recursion are not analysed; a loop whose body always exits through an `if` is still reported, because proving that needs the dataflow this rule does not do.

rules.title: Do not name a declaration after a reserved keyword
rules.summary: A declaration is named after a reserved C# keyword and can only be written with an `@` escape, so every mention of it reads as a verbatim string, a typo or a keyword until the reader checks.
rules.rationale: `@class`, `@new` and `@event` are legal and cost the reader a stop every time. The `@` on a reserved keyword is never a disambiguation the language asked for; it is the only spelling available once the name was chosen, so the finding is about the name. No fix is offered: renaming a declaration means renaming every reference, which is a refactoring rather than a text edit.

examples.bad: void Register(Type @class, EventInfo @event) { }
examples.good: void Register(Type declaredType, EventInfo declaredEvent) { }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Reserved keywords only, and that is what keeps the rule off load-bearing escapes.** Every `@` a language feature can *require* is on a contextual keyword — `@field` once `field` became the backing-field keyword, `@value` in an accessor, `@extension`, `@record`, `@var`, `@async`, `@await` — and a contextual keyword is a legal identifier without the escape, so an escape on one is disambiguation rather than a name to change. None of them is reported. Only the declaring identifier is reported, never a reference to it: a name that comes from another assembly must be escaped at every use site and the author cannot rename it, so reporting uses would be reporting something nobody can fix, and it would multiply one finding by its call count. Constructors and destructors are skipped because their identifier repeats the type's, which is already reported once. Namespace name parts and query continuations are not examined. Verbatim strings, interpolated verbatim strings and `@` inside documentation or comments are not identifiers and are never seen.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ ReSharper publishes this one as an `.editorconfig` key with no inspection id in its issue-type dump, so `resharperId` carries the id that derives to the real key — `resharper_escaped_keyword_highlighting`, which the export sets to `warning`. Skala defaults the rule to `suggestion`, so `--resharper-severities` raises it: an escaped keyword compiles and runs correctly, and the cost is entirely to the reader.

rules.title: An `Enum` constraint has no `struct` beside it
rules.summary: `where T : Enum` admits `System.Enum` itself, so `T` is a reference type whose `default` is `null` and which no enum API accepts.
rules.rationale: `where T : struct, Enum` is what the author of `where T : Enum` meant, and the difference is one type argument: `System.Enum`, the abstract base class. It satisfies the bare constraint by identity, so inside the method `T` is not known to be a value type — `default(T)` is `null`, every use boxes, and the type argument names a class that is not an enum and has no values. The BCL agrees: `Enum.GetValues<TEnum>()`, `Enum.TryParse<TEnum>`, `Enum.IsDefined<TEnum>` and `Enum.GetName<TEnum>` are all declared `where TEnum : struct, Enum`, so a method constrained the weaker way cannot call any of them and has to fall back on the boxing, reflective overloads it was written to avoid. Adding `struct` costs one keyword and makes the signature say what the body already assumes.

examples.bad:
public static string[] Names<T>() where T : Enum =>
    Enum.GetNames(typeof(T));
examples.good:
public static string[] Names<T>() where T : struct, Enum =>
    Enum.GetNames<T>();

rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The reason this rule exists is not the reason the proposal gave.** Issue #261 says `where T : Enum` permits `Nullable<TEnum>`; it does not. The compiler rejects `Name<Colour?>(…)` against a bare `Enum` constraint with CS0312, "the nullable type does not satisfy the constraint of 'System.Enum'", which was measured before the rule was written rather than reasoned about. The one type argument `struct` actually excludes is `System.Enum` itself (CS0453 once `struct` is there), and that is the whole of the finding — a reference type, `default(T)` of `null`, no values, and rejected by every generic `Enum` API in the BCL.

The rule fires only on a constraint clause whose `Enum` resolves to `System.Enum` and which carries no `struct`. Four clause shapes are skipped because adding `struct` to them does not compile, and a fix that does not compile is worse than a miss: `unmanaged` (already a stricter value-type constraint), `notnull` (CS8716 forbids the combination), `class` (`where T : class, Enum` is a deliberate, if narrow, statement about reference types), and `new()` (CS0451 forbids `struct` with `new()` — `struct` implies it, but repairing that needs a second edit and this rule makes one). `where T : Enum?` is left alone: the annotation says the author considered nullability and answered. A user type named `Enum` is not `System.Enum` and is not reported, which is why the rule is semantic. A clause containing a preprocessor directive is skipped, the same reason `SK6003` skips one, and so is one where the `Enum` is not the first constraint — CS0406 says it always is in legal code, so requiring it keeps the insertion point provable from the one node the rule looked at.

⚠ **The fix is `fixIsSafe: false`, against the proposal's `true`.** Narrowing a constraint on a generic signature is a source-breaking change whose breakage lands in files this edit does not touch: a caller passing `System.Enum` stops compiling (CS0453), and a method that implements an interface member may no longer match its declared constraints (CS0425). Every one of those is a compiler error rather than a silent behaviour change, so the edit is never dangerous — but "apply without review" is a promise about somebody else's build, and Skala cannot see the rest of the solution from one syntax tree. Review is the honest requirement.

rules.title: A type is named like an exception and is not one
rules.summary: The `Exception` suffix is a promise that `catch (SomethingException)` will work, and a type that does not derive from `System.Exception` cannot keep it.
rules.rationale: `Exception` at the end of a type name is not decoration; it is the one naming convention in .NET that a language construct depends on. A reader who sees `PaymentDeclinedException` writes `catch (PaymentDeclinedException)`, and if the type does not derive from `System.Exception` that line does not compile — the name has cost them the time it takes to find out why. Everything else that keys on the suffix is misled the same way: `throw`, exception filters, logging that unwraps an `AggregateException`, analyzers that check exception design, and the reviewer skimming a diff. The type is either an exception and should say so in its base list, or it is not one and should not claim the suffix. Neither answer is a mechanical edit, which is why the rule has no fix.
rules.falsePositives:
**The suffix, never the substring.** `ExceptionHandler`, `ExceptionFilter`, `ExceptionPolicy`, `ExceptionDispatcher` and `ExceptionExtensions` are all correctly named and none of them is an exception — and none of them is reported, because each ends in the word that says what it really is. That is the whole of the containment question: a type *about* exceptions puts `Exception` in the middle and its own noun at the end, and only a type *claiming to be* one puts `Exception` last. Nothing here looks for the substring.

**Interfaces are out of scope.** An interface cannot derive from `System.Exception`, so `IRetryableException` is not a mistake this rule could ask anyone to correct — the finding would have no available answer. `enum` and `delegate` declarations are excluded for the same reason. Classes, structs, records and record structs are all reported: a `struct` named `…Exception` cannot be one either, but there the name is the thing to change and the message says so.
