Choosing between them is exactly the design judgement the finding is asking somebody to make.

rules.title: An abstract type declares nothing to implement
rules.summary: `abstract` says both "do not instantiate this" and "a derived type completes it", and a class with no hooks, nothing `protected` and no base is only saying the first.
rules.rationale: A reader who meets `abstract class Report` expects to find the part a subclass has to supply, and goes looking for it. When there is no `abstract` member, no `virtual` member, nothing `protected` and no base type, there is nothing to find: no derived type is required to provide anything, none is offered anything it could not get from an instance, and the keyword's only effect is that `new Report()` does not compile. That is a real intent and there are three better ways to state it — a `static` class if the members are all static, an interface if the members are all contracts, or a concrete class if instantiating it is fine — and each of the three tells the next reader something. `abstract` alone tells them to keep looking for a hook that is not there.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The `protected` exemption is the one carrying the rule, and a protected constructor is its usual form.** A base class that shares state through a `protected` constructor, a `protected` field or a `protected` helper is arranged for derivation whether or not it declares anything abstract, and reporting it would be reporting the most ordinary base class in C#. `virtual` is exempt for the same reason and counts as much as `abstract`: "you may override this" is an extension point somebody put there deliberately, and a visitor base whose every method is an empty `virtual` is the canonical shape of one. What is left after those two exemptions is a class with public and private concrete members, no base and no derived-only surface at all.

⚠ **A nested type deriving from the containing type is an exemption, and the sweep found it rather than the design did.** `abstract class Shape { private Shape() { } public sealed class Circle : Shape { … } }` is how C# spells a closed hierarchy: no `abstract`, no `virtual` and nothing `protected`, because the derived types are right there in the body — the derivation surface stated as directly as it can be. The first version of the rule reported it, which was found by running the rule over its own sibling fixtures. The base list is matched on the written name rather than on a symbol, which keeps the rule syntactic and costs a miss where a nested type derives from something else sharing the container's simple name.

**A base list on the abstract class itself is an exemption on its own, and it is why the rule is syntactic.** An abstract class that derives from something may be inheriting abstract members it deliberately does not implement, or carrying interface members a derived type must supply — both are genuine things to implement, and neither is visible in this declaration. Declining every one of them removes the only question that needed a symbol, so the rule runs under `--load=loose`. The cost is a miss on a middle-of-hierarchy class that really does add nothing.

⚠ **Records are out of scope entirely.** An `abstract record` is overwhelmingly the root of a closed hierarchy, and its generated members — the copy constructor, `EqualsContract`, the printing members — are the derivation surface a hand-written class has to declare for itself. There is no shape there this rule could read as an omission, so `record` and `record struct` are not analysed at all rather than filtered later.

**`partial` is never reported.** The other part may declare the abstract member, or may not exist yet because a generator writes it — the same single exemption that keeps `SK6023` out of every source-generated codebase.

**A type carrying an attribute is exempt.** A framework that requires a base class, a generator, or a serializer reads the attribute, so the declaration's shape is not the whole story.

**An `abstract class Foo { }` with no members at all is not reported here.** That is `SK6023`'s finding, and billing one declaration twice for one omission would double it in every report.

**The shape that stays genuinely arguable** is a base class whose members are all `public` and concrete and whose author wants only to forbid `new Report()` — `abstract class Shape { public string Name { get; init; } }` with subclasses that add nothing abstract. It is reported, the author's intent is real, and a `protected` constructor — which such a class almost always has, because that is how the name gets set — takes it out of scope. The rule ships at `suggestion` because of the ones that do not.

⚠ **The implicit constructor is not a member.** An abstract class gets a compiler-generated `protected` parameterless constructor, and the rule reads *declared* members only. Counting the generated one would exempt every abstract class in the language and leave the rule matching nothing.

⚠ **No fix.** The three repairs — drop `abstract`, make it `static`, make it an interface — are three different answers to "what was this type for", each of which changes the public surface in a different direction. Guessing between them would be guessing at intent, and the finding says look at this rather than what to do.

rules.title: A type has only private constructors and is not static
rules.summary: Nothing outside the type can construct it, and nothing inside the file does either, so no caller can ever obtain an instance.
rules.rationale: A private constructor is a normal thing to write: a singleton hands out one instance, a factory validates before constructing, a static holder predates `static class`. Each of those puts something beside the constructor — a `new` of the type inside the type, or a nested type deriving from it. The finding is the same private constructor with none of that: no creation anywhere it could legally appear, no derivation, and no `static` to say the type was never meant to be instantiated. The type compiles, ships, and cannot be reached, and no compiler diagnostic says so — the members read as a public API that no caller can ever call. `SK6003` reports the opposite error on abstract types; this is the same question about instantiability from the other end.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The reachability test is a proof, not a heuristic, and that is why it reads the whole file.** A private constructor is accessible only inside the containing type's body, so for a type that is not `partial` every legal `new` of it and every legal derivation from it is in this one syntax tree. A creation or a base list anywhere in the file withdraws the finding, which covers a singleton's `static readonly Foo Instance = new();`, a `static Foo Create()`, a nested builder, and a `Parse` — none of them needs to be recognised as a pattern, because all of them create the type.

⚠ **Nesting opens access inward, not outward, and the first draft of this rule had it backwards.** A nested type reaches its *container's* private constructor — a nested builder calling `new Pipeline(…)`, a nested case deriving from its container — and that is what makes scanning the file rather than the candidate's own body necessary. The reverse does not hold: a container calling a *nested* type's private constructor is **CS0122**, which was found by compiling it rather than reasoned about, and the fixture that asserted it had to be replaced. `private` limits access to the type that declares the member and to what is nested inside it, in no other direction.

**`partial` is never reported**, and here that is not caution but the proof failing: the other part may declare a public constructor or create the type, and it is exactly where "the file holds every access to a private member" stops being true.

⚠ **`abstract` is excluded, and it is the exemption most worth stating.** An abstract class with a private constructor is a hierarchy closed to its own nested types — how C# spells a discriminated union — and is a deliberate, increasingly common design rather than an unreachable type. `record` and `struct` are excluded for a flatter reason: a positional record has a public primary constructor, and a struct always has an implicit parameterless one, so a private constructor never makes either unreachable.

**A type carrying an attribute is exempt, and so is a constructor carrying one.** `[JsonConstructor]` names a private constructor for a serializer to call, and a container, a generator or a `[Serializable]` marker each reaches a type through a caller in no syntax tree at all.

**`typeof(Foo)` in the same file withdraws the finding.** Beside a private constructor, that is what reflection looks like from here — `Activator.CreateInstance(typeof(Foo), nonPublic: true)`, a container registration by type, a test creating an instance the API does not offer. The rule cannot follow it and does not guess.

⚠ **Reflection from another file is the false positive that remains, and nothing here can see it.** `Activator.CreateInstance` on a type obtained by name, a DI registration built from assembly scanning, and `RuntimeHelpers.GetUninitializedObject` all produce instances of a type this rule has just called unreachable. They are rare, they are exactly the code that should carry a comment saying so, and they are the case to baseline.

**At least one *declared* constructor is required.** A class that declares none has an implicit public one and is closed to nothing; matching on "has no public constructor" instead would report every ordinary class in the language.

⚠ **No fix, and the reason is not that no edit exists — it is that one exists for only some of the findings.** The static-holder shape, a private parameterless constructor with nothing but static members beside it, has an obvious two-edit repair: add `static`, delete the constructor. The general shape — a private constructor and instance members — has none, because "make it reachable" is a choice between a factory, a public constructor and deleting the type. Skala's fixture harness asserts that *every* finding of a rule declaring `hasFix: true` carries edits, so a rule cannot offer a fix for one shape and not the other, and splitting the concept across two ids to get one would be allocating a permanent number for the sake of an edit. The finding names the three repairs and lets a person pick.

rules.title: A public constant is baked into every caller
rules.summary: The compiler copies a `const` into the consuming assembly, so changing it and shipping only your own assembly leaves every caller on the old value with no error anywhere.
rules.rationale: ⚠ **This is a property of how the value is distributed, not of how the declaration is written.** The compiler does not emit a field read for `Limits.MaxRetries`; it emits the literal `3`, into the *consumer's* assembly. Ship version 2 of the library with the value changed to `5`, and every assembly that was built against version 1 keeps `3` — the load succeeds, no binding redirect fires, no analyzer complains, and the two halves of the program disagree about a number they both believe they read from one place. It is the one versioning hazard in .NET with no diagnostic at all behind it: a renamed member is a `MissingMethodException`, a changed signature is a `MissingMethodException`, and a changed constant is silence. `static readonly` is read from the field at run time and does not have this property, at the cost of one indirection and a type initializer. The reason to keep a `const` public is that its value is part of the contract and can never change — a protocol magic number, a format version, a mathematical constant — and that is a claim worth making on purpose rather than by default.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The rule cannot tell a value that will never change from one that is merely constant today, and that is the whole false-positive story.** A protocol magic number, a wire format version, `"\r\n"`, a mathematical constant and a spec-mandated field width are all correctly `public const`: the value is part of the contract, so a caller holding the old copy holds the right one. A retry count, a buffer size, a timeout, a URL and a display string are the opposite, and nothing in the declaration separates the two. The rule ships at `suggestion` for this reason, and the answer for a value that really is fixed is a suppression with the sentence saying why.

⚠ **The harm needs an assembly boundary, and the rule cannot see whether there is one.** In a solution rebuilt end to end on every commit, `const` is fine — everything is recompiled, so every copy is refreshed at once. The hazard is real for a library that ships independently of its consumers, which is the general case and the one the rule assumes. An application with no reference surface is where a suppression is cheapest.

**`internal` and `private` constants are never reported, and neither is a `public const` inside an `internal` type.** Visibility is computed by walking the field's accessibility *and* every containing type's, because a `public const` that cannot leave the assembly is never copied anywhere compiled separately. That walk is the difference between this rule and one that reports every `public const` in a program. `InternalsVisibleTo` does not change the answer: the friend assembly is in the same solution and rebuilt with it.

**Constants in an interface are excluded.** A `static readonly` field in an interface is legal and is not the same declaration — it changes what implementers see and when the runtime initializes it — so the one-token fix would not be the repair it claims to be.

⚠ **The fix is `fixIsSafe: false`, and the breakage it can cause lands in files the edit does not touch.** A `const` is usable where the language demands a compile-time constant and a `static readonly` field is not: an attribute argument (CS0182), an optional parameter's default value (CS1736), a `case` label or constant pattern (CS0150), another `const`'s initializer (CS0133), and `goto case`. Every one of those is a compiler error rather than a silent behaviour change, so the edit is never dangerous — but each is a caller's build, possibly in another repository, and "apply without review" is a promise this rule cannot make. Two smaller consequences go with it: the value stops being folded at compile time, so a comparison against it is no longer a constant expression; and the type gains a static initializer where it may have had none.

⚠ **There is deliberately no local guard against those positions.** The rule could refuse to report a `const` that the same file uses in an attribute argument or a parameter default, and it does not — because the identical breakage across an assembly boundary is precisely what this rule exists to say it cannot see, and a guard that catches only the visible half would make the finding look better checked than it is. `fixIsSafe: false` is the honest statement, and it is one statement rather than two.

**One finding per declaration, not per declarator.** `public const int A = 1, B = 2;` has one `const` token and one edit; two findings would carry the same replacement twice. A declaration whose `const` token carries a preprocessor directive is skipped, for the reason `SK6003` skips one: the token the fix names may not be the token every branch compiles.

rules.title: The disposable field is not disposed by `Dispose`
rules.summary: The type implements `IDisposable`, constructs a disposable field, and nothing in the type ever disposes it.
rules.rationale: This is the ownership bug that looks finished. `SK3502` reports a type that owns a disposable and is not disposable, which reads as work somebody has not got to yet; here the interface is declared, the `Dispose` is written, and the handle is still never released — so the type reads as one that cleans up after itself to every caller, every reviewer and every tool that checks only for the declaration. What shows up instead is a file that cannot be reopened or a pool that empties, in a process that disposed everything it was supposed to.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Disjoint from `SK3502` by construction rather than by deduplication.** This rule requires the owner to implement `IDisposable`; `SK3502` reports only where the owner does *not* implement the contract its field offers. The two predicates cannot both hold for one field, so neither declares `supersedes` — which dedupes on a shared span and would suppress one of the two reports rather than leaving each rule's finding a property of that rule. ⚠ **"Never disposed" is asked of the whole type, not of `Dispose`'s body.** The documented pattern puts the work in `Dispose(bool disposing)`, and a private `Shutdown()` called from `Dispose` is just as correct; reading only the entry point would report every faithful implementation of the pattern. Any `Dispose`, `DisposeAsync` or `Close` on the field, anywhere in the declaration, withdraws the finding. ⚠ **Ownership is inferred exactly the way `SK3502` infers it** — a direct object creation in the field's own initializer. A constructor-injected, factory-returned or static field is not reported, because whether this type owns it is not knowable here. ⚠ **Any reference the rule does not recognise withdraws it.** Passing the field as an argument, assigning it again, returning it or casting it are all ways the resource leaves the type, and the rule cannot follow it; only plain member and element reads keep the finding. ⚠ Private fields only, and non-partial types only: a `protected` field may be disposed by a derived type and the other half of a `partial` is not in this tree. A nullable field is skipped because the repair there is `?.Dispose()` and the null case is a decision rather than an edit. ⚠ **The finding is withheld unless the repair has somewhere to land**: the type's own parameterless `Dispose` must have a block body. An expression-bodied, abstract or inherited `Dispose` is the same bug and is not reported. The fix is unsafe because disposal order between owned resources is a property of the type that no edit can read.

rules.title: The `DisposeAsync` override never calls the base implementation
rules.summary: An `override` of `DisposeAsync` or `DisposeAsyncCore` never reaches the implementation it replaced, so the base type's asynchronous cleanup stops happening.
rules.rationale: Asynchronous disposal is a chain: `DisposeAsync` calls a virtual `DisposeAsyncCore`, and each override finishes by calling the one it overrode. An override that skips the base breaks the chain at that link — the base type's final flush, its graceful close, its return to a pool simply stop running. Nothing says so. There is no compiler diagnostic, no test that fails, and the type still satisfies `IAsyncDisposable`; the resource is released when the process ends, or not at all. `CA1063` pins the synchronous pattern and `CA2215` pins the synchronous base call, and neither has an asynchronous counterpart.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Every finding is provable, and the guards are what makes that true rather than likely.** The overridden method must be declared in *this* compilation and its body must contain at least one invocation. A base in another assembly is a body the rule never reads, and a base whose body is `ValueTask.CompletedTask`, `default` or an empty block loses nothing by being skipped; both withdraw. ⚠ **The cost is a stated gap rather than a hidden one**: a type deriving from a framework base with a real `DisposeAsyncCore` is exactly the case this rule does not cover, and widening it would mean reporting on code the rule cannot see. ⚠ An abstract base has no implementation to lose and is not reported. ⚠ **Any `base.` call at all withdraws it**, not only a call to this method: an override reaching the base type through a different member is participating in the chain in a way the rule has no business second-guessing. ⚠ An override whose entire body is a `throw` is refusing the operation, not forgetting the base. Only the non-generic `ValueTask` and `Task` shapes are matched, and the containing type must implement `IAsyncDisposable`. ⚠ **No fix, and that is a decision.** The call goes last in an override and first in a wrapper, it must be awaited in some bodies and returned in others, and where it belongs among the override's own cleanup is an ordering decision that no edit can read off the text.

rules.title: The `ref struct` owns a disposable and cannot declare it
rules.summary: A `ref struct` constructs a field whose `ref struct` type is disposable through the pattern rule alone, and declares no `Dispose()` of its own.
rules.rationale: This is the one ownership shape the rest of the family cannot reach. A `ref struct` whose only disposal contract is a public parameterless `Dispose()` is disposable through the language's pattern rule and through nothing else — it implements no interface, so `SK3502`, which asks whether the owner implements the contract the field offers, has no contract to ask about and stays silent by construction. The owner constructs the resource, holds it, and offers its own callers no `using` to write: the release simply never happens, and no analyzer in the family reports it.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The field's type must implement neither `IDisposable` nor `IAsyncDisposable`, and that is the disjointness guard rather than a limitation.** C# 13 lets a `ref struct` implement an interface, and where the field's type does, the ownership is one `SK3502` can see and report; without the test both rules would speak about one field. `supersedes` is the wrong instrument for that — `Supersession.Apply` suppresses the *superseded* finding on a shared span — so the two are made disjoint by construction and a fixture pins it. ⚠ **Ownership is proved, not assumed**: the field must be assigned from a direct object creation, in its own initializer or in a constructor. A field assigned from a constructor parameter is a borrowed resource whose lifetime belongs to the caller, and disposing it here would close something somebody else is still holding. ⚠ The disposal contract asked for is exactly the one `using` binds to: a public, parameterless, non-static `Dispose()` returning `void`. A type declaring only `Dispose(bool)` is reported, because `using` cannot bind to it. ⚠ Partial types are skipped, because the other half may carry the `Dispose` and is not in this tree. ⚠ **No fix.** A correct `Dispose()` decides which fields it releases, in what order, and whether a second call is safe — and the repair may instead be that this type should not own the resource at all. No edit answers that.

rules.title: The async iterator is enumerated without `await foreach`
rules.summary: A method returning `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is called as a whole statement and the result dropped, so the iterator's body never runs.
rules.rationale: An `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` handed to a plain `foreach` does not compile, which is why the mistake takes this shape instead: the iterator is invoked and the result discarded. That compiles, warns about nothing, and does nothing — an async iterator does not start until something enumerates it, so not one statement of the method's body executes. The call reads as work being done and no work is done, which is the failure that survives every test that only checks for an exception.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Only where the repair compiles.** The nearest enclosing method, local function or lambda must already be `async`, and the statement must sit directly in a block, in a position an `await` is legal in — not a `lock` body, a constructor, an operator or an expression tree. In a synchronous method the same call is the same bug and is not reported, because the repair there is to make the method `async`, which changes its signature and every caller with it; that is the line `SK3503` draws and it is drawn here in the same place. ⚠ **The finding is withheld when `_` is already in scope**, because the rewrite names the loop variable and shadowing an existing local is CS0136 — a fix that parses and does not compile is the one failure a fixing tool may not have. ⚠ **Only the invoked-and-dropped shape.** An `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` bound to a variable that is then never enumerated is the same bug and is not matched: proving that a variable is never enumerated needs flow analysis this rule does not do, and a wrong answer there deletes work rather than adding it. An explicit `_ = ProcessAsync(items);` is not reported either — the discard says the author meant to drop it, and if they were wrong the repair is a decision rather than an edit. ⚠ **The fix is unsafe by declaration**, and not because the edit is uncertain: it turns a statement that does nothing into one that runs the iterator to completion. That is the repair, and it is still a behaviour change somebody should read.

rules.title: The method is `async` only to return an awaited task
rules.summary: The method's whole body is `return await X()`, so the `async` state machine exists only to hand back a task the method already had.
rules.rationale: An `async` method compiles to a state machine, an allocation and a resumption path. Where the entire body is one `await` whose result is returned unchanged, all of that exists to give the caller a task the method was holding already. Returning it directly removes the machinery and does the same work.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The fix is unsafe and the reason is not the edit.** Eliding the `await` moves exceptions from the returned task to the call — a method that used to fault its task now throws synchronously, at a place the caller may not be catching — and drops the method from every stack trace the task carries. Both are behaviour, both are usually acceptable, and neither is a decision a tool makes. ⚠ **It is outright wrong inside a `using`, which is what `SK3007` reports, and the two are disjoint by construction.** The body matched here must be a *single* statement that is the `return await`, or a single expression body: a `using` declaration needs a statement before the return, and a `using` statement makes the block's one statement a `using` rather than a `return`, so no shape this rule reports can contain one. `supersedes` would be the wrong instrument regardless — `Supersession.Apply` suppresses the *superseded* finding, which is the one carrying the remedy. ⚠ **The operand's type must be the declared return type, not merely awaitable to it.** `await GetValueTask()` inside an `async Task<int>` is legal and `return GetValueTask()` is not; the same test is what excludes `.ConfigureAwait(false)`, whose type is a configured awaitable rather than a task. ⚠ **A nested `await` in the operand withdraws it**: `return await Read(await Open());` would leave an `await` in a method that is no longer `async`, which is CS4032 — a fix that parses and does not compile. ⚠ Only ordinary methods and local functions; `partial`, `abstract` and `extern` are skipped, and lambdas are not matched at all. ⚠ A comment between `async` and the return type, or between `await` and its operand, withdraws the finding rather than being deleted with the keyword.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_replace_async_with_task_return_highlighting = none` and this rule defaults to `suggestion`. ReSharper ships the inspection switched off, which is a reasonable default for a change that moves where exceptions surface; doc 00's ninth non-negotiable says a severity comes from what the rule means rather than from how loud it is, and what this one means is "there is machinery here doing nothing" — a suggestion. Reading the ReSharper key (off by default, doc 03 § "Severities") would silence it.

rules.title: The `with` expression or object initializer is empty
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ ReSharper rates `RedundantWithExpression` a *suggestion* and `RedundantEmptyObjectOrCollectionInitializer` a *warning*; Skala reports one concept at `warning` and reading `resharper_redundant_with_expression_highlighting` therefore lowers both. The severity split is the same observation this rule's `fixIsSafe: false` records: the empty initializer is nothing, and the empty `with` is an allocation somebody may have meant.
rules.summary: A pair of initializer braces that sets nothing: `new Foo { }` is `new Foo()`, and `x with { }` copies a record and changes nothing.
rules.rationale: Empty braces read as a list somebody is about to fill in and stay in the file for years after nobody is. `new Foo { }` is two characters of ceremony over `new Foo()`. `x with { }` is more than ceremony — `with` invokes the record's compiler-generated copy constructor, so it allocates a whole instance in order to produce a value equal to the one it was given.

examples.bad:
var options = new JsonSerializerOptions { };
var copy = original with { };
examples.good:
var options = new JsonSerializerOptions();
var copy = original;

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The fix is declared unsafe, and the empty `with` is the whole reason.** `new Foo { }` → `new Foo()` is a pure deletion with no observable effect at all, but `x with { }` → `x` is not: the copy constructor produces a *distinct* instance, so removing it aliases a clone the author may have written in order to mutate it, and it removes the `NullReferenceException` a null operand would have thrown. Splitting one concept into two safety classes would have been the alternative; the conservative reading of the whole rule is the cheaper mistake. ⚠ Only the two initializer kinds that mean "and then set these members" are matched. An empty array initializer belongs to an `ArrayCreationExpression`, which this rule never sees — `new int[] { }` cannot lose its braces and still compile. An anonymous type is a different node again: `new { }` has no `new ()` to become. ⚠ A creation with no argument list *grows* one, because `new Foo` is not an expression; a creation that already has arguments keeps them, and `new()` target-typed creation is matched through the same path. ⚠ A comment or a preprocessor directive between the braces withdraws the finding: an empty initializer holding a note is a note about why it is empty, and the fix deletes the braces wholesale.

rules.title: The string call produces the string it was given
rules.summary: `ToString()` on a string, `foreach` over `ToCharArray()`, `string.Format` of a literal with no placeholders, an interpolated string with no holes, and a verbatim prefix that escapes nothing.
rules.rationale: Two of the five are allocations rather than noise. `s.ToCharArray()` copies the whole string so that `foreach` can walk what `string` already enumerates by index, and `string.Format` runs a format parser over a format that has no items. The other three are the reader's cost: a `$` promises a hole, a `@` promises something that needs escaping, and a `.ToString()` on a string promises a conversion. Each one is a sentence that turns out to say nothing, and a reader has to finish it before finding that out.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Each branch is guarded by what the deletion would mean, not by what it would look like.** An interpolated string is reported only where the compiler was converting it to `string`: `FormattableString fs = $"a";` and every interpolated-string-handler overload accept `$"a"` and reject `"a"`, and nothing in the syntax separates the two. `string.Format` is reported only where the literal holds no brace at all, because `string.Format("{{0}}")` returns `{0}` and the literal returns `{{0}}` — the shape that looks most obviously safe is the one that is not. A verbatim prefix is reported only where the body holds no backslash, no doubled quote and no newline, since the prefix is what makes each of those mean what it means. ⚠ `s.ToString();` as a whole statement is the null-check idiom and is never reported: the result is discarded, so the dereference *is* the call, and `s;` is not an expression statement. ⚠ A receiver the compiler's flow analysis says may be null is left alone in both call shapes, because `s.ToString()` is typed `string` where `s` is `string?` and the deletion is where `CS8600` would come from. ⚠ **Three of the family's eight inspections are deliberately not covered.** `RedundantToStringCallForValueType` is not: `$"{d}"` on an `IFormattable` calls `ToString(null, provider)` where `d.ToString()` calls `ToString()`, and a supplied provider makes those two different strings. `RedundantStringInterpolation`'s single-hole form is not: `$"{x}"` is `""` where `x` is null and `x` is null, which is a change of value and not of spelling. `RedundantStringType` and `RedundantVerbatimPrefix`'s identifier form are not covered either — the identifier form neighbours `SK2034`. ⚠ The receiver's type is read from the symbol and never from the written name, so `((object)s).ToString()` and `count.ToString()` are both left alone.

rules.title: The argument or signature element is redundant
rules.summary: A trailing argument that restates the parameter's default, a delegate creation the conversion would have performed, or lambda parameter types the target already declares.
rules.rationale: An argument restating a default is a value that silently stops tracking the default the day it changes — the same hazard `optional-and-params-hazards` reports from the declaration side, seen from the call. `new EventHandler(Foo)` is an allocation as well as noise: the method group converts to the delegate on its own, and writing the conversion out produces exactly the same object through more text.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Deleting an argument can change which method is called, and the rule asks the compiler rather than reasoning about it.** With `Foo(int a, int b = 0)` beside `Foo(int a)`, `Foo(1, 0)` and `Foo(1)` are calls to two different methods and nothing about the argument says so. Every finding re-binds the shortened call speculatively and withdraws unless the same symbol comes back, which is the guard Roslyn's own `IDE0004` family exists to remind everybody about. ⚠ **A caller-info parameter is excluded and looks exactly like the shape that is not.** Passing `null` to a `[CallerMemberName] string name = null` restates the default in the source and is the only thing keeping the value null: omit it and the compiler substitutes the caller's name. The same applies to `[CallerLineNumber]`, `[CallerFilePath]` and `[CallerArgumentExpression]`. ⚠ Positional arguments only — a named argument need not be last and need not fill the parameter its position names, so "the trailing argument's parameter" stops being a fact. A `params` parameter, a `ref`/`out`/`in` argument, and any argument whose value is not a compile-time constant equal to the default are all excluded; `default(SomeStruct)` is not a constant, so a struct default is never matched. Consecutive trailing defaults are removed in **one** edit, longest suffix first, because one at a time would make the rule fire on its own output. ⚠ The two conversion shapes avoid overload resolution instead of answering it: both are reported only where the target type is written down — an explicitly typed variable or an assignment — because as an *argument* a method group or a lambda can be the thing that picks the overload. A method group only, never a delegate value (`new EventHandler(other)` is a copy) and never a lambda. Lambda parameter types are compared **including nullability**: `Func<string?, int> f = (string x) => x.Length;` compiles, and dropping the written type would introduce the `CS8602` the author wrote it to avoid. ⚠ **Four of the family's seven inspections are not covered**: `RedundantExplicitParamsArrayCreation` (`Foo(new object[] { arr })` and `Foo(arr)` pass the array in two different roles), `RedundantCallerArgumentExpressionDefaultValue`, `UnusedAnonymousMethodSignature` and `RedundantImmediateDelegateInvocation`. Constructor arguments and attribute arguments are not matched either; only invocations are.

rules.title: The syntax is redundant
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ ReSharper rates `RedundantAttributeParentheses` a *hint* and rates `RedundantAnonymousTypePropertyName`, one of the other eight shapes under this id, a *warning*. Skala reports the concept at `suggestion`, so reading `resharper_redundant_attribute_parentheses_highlighting` raises the whole concept to whatever that one key says.
rules.summary: Nine token-level deletions: an empty attribute argument list, a single lambda parameter's parentheses, parentheses around a whole pattern, a semicolon after a braced declaration, braces around a one-argument collection element, an anonymous-type property name that restates the expression, `ascending`, a range bound that is already the default, and an empty property pattern under a type.
rules.rationale: Each one is a token the grammar allows and the reader has to account for. None of them is a judgement call: the deletion is proved by the shape, there is no semantic component at all, and the fix is the shortest edit in the catalogue. Doc 17 § "A large share of the 580 is cheap" is about exactly this family — the mechanical cleanups a Rider user does not notice they rely on until they are gone.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`SK0209` is not being duplicated, and the check was made rather than assumed.** That rule removes redundant *expression* parentheses through `resharper_parentheses_redundancy_style`, and it matches `ParenthesizedExpressionSyntax` and nothing else. The three parenthesis shapes here are an attribute argument list, a lambda parameter list and a parenthesized *pattern* — three different nodes, none of which that option reaches. ⚠ **Purely syntactic on purpose**: no branch reads the semantic model, so this is the one rule in the `SK023x` family that still runs, and is therefore still measurable, under `--load=loose` where a dependency-less source slice makes every semantic guard withdraw. ⚠ Pattern parentheses are removed only where the pattern is the *whole* of its position — under an `is`, a switch arm, a `case` label or a subpattern. Inside an `and`/`or` the parentheses can be the precedence, and proving otherwise is a re-parse this rule deliberately does not do. ⚠ A trailing declaration semicolon is reported only where braces are present: `record R(int X);` has no body, and there the semicolon is the terminator. ⚠ A lambda parameter with a type, a modifier, an attribute or a default value keeps its parentheses — the typed case belongs to `SK0232`, which *produces* this shape's output, so the two are disjoint by construction. ⚠ A range bound is matched on the literal `0` read from the source, never on a constant value: a named constant that happens to be zero is a name somebody chose. ⚠ An anonymous-type property name is dropped only for the two spellings C# infers a name from, so `x.Foo<int>` is left alone even where the written name matches. ⚠ **Four of the family's thirteen inspections are not covered.** `RedundantDiscardDesignation` is left out on purpose: `out var _` becomes `out _` only where nothing named `_` is in scope, and answering that needs a symbol lookup that would make the whole rule semantic. `RedundantFixedPointerDeclaration` is unsafe-code-only. `RedundantPropertyParentheses` and `RedundantArrayLowerBoundSpecification` could not be identified from the export with enough confidence to write a guard for them.

rules.title: The cast or type argument is redundant
rules.summary: A cast whose operand already has the cast's type, explicit method type arguments inference reproduces exactly, an array size that repeats the element count, and tuple component names the declared type already carries.
rules.rationale: Each one is a conversion that converts nothing, and each is read as if it might. A cast makes a reader ask what the operand was before it; explicit type arguments make them ask what inference would have chosen; an array size makes them count the elements to see whether the two agree.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **A cast is not redundant merely because the types allow removing it, and this rule is written around that sentence.** `var x = (long)1;` types `x` as `long` and `var x = 1;` types it as `int`. `M((object)s)` and `M(s)` call different overloads. `flag ? (long)a : b` infers a different type once the cast is gone. Roslyn's own `IDE0004` is the standing example of getting this wrong, so Skala covers the one subset where none of those questions can be asked: an **identity** conversion, where the operand's type and the cast's type are the same symbol — checked with `SymbolEqualityComparer.IncludeNullability` and confirmed by `ClassifyConversion(...).IsIdentity`. The expression's type is then unchanged by the deletion, so nothing downstream of it can change either. ⚠ **Every widening, narrowing and boxing cast is therefore deliberately uncovered**, including the upcast that is most of what `RedundantCast` reports in practice. That is a smaller rule on purpose; the negative fixture set records each declined shape. ⚠ Nullability is not a detail here: `(string)maybeNull` is typed `string` where its operand is `string?`, so the cast is what tells the flow analysis what the author knows, and a `var` declared from it would change type without it. ⚠ Tuples are excluded from the cast branch entirely and handled by the component-name branch, because `((int a, int b))(1, 2)` and `((int, int))(1, 2)` differ in the names the result carries. ⚠ Explicit method type arguments are removed only where re-binding the call without them reaches the **identical constructed method** — the same definition with different inferred type arguments does not count. ⚠ An array size is matched for one dimension only: a jagged or rectangular creation has sizes whose relationship to the initializer is not the flat count this compares against. ⚠ Tuple component names are dropped only under a **written** tuple type. Under `var` the names come from the literal and deleting them deletes them from the variable's type, and no semantic query separates those two cases because the resulting type is identical. ⚠ **Four of the family's eight inspections are not covered**: `RedundantExplicitArrayCreation` (`new object[] { "a", "b" }` infers `string[]` once the type is dropped), `RedundantExplicitNullableCreation`, `RedundantTypeArgumentsInsideNameof` and `PreferExplicitlyProvidedTupleComponentName`, which asks for the opposite of what this rule does.

rules.title: A class with `[TestMethod]` members carries no `[TestClass]`
rules.summary: A class declares MSTest `[TestMethod]` members and is not itself marked `[TestClass]`, so MSTest discovers none of them and the suite is green because nothing ran.
rules.rationale: This is the worst failure a test can have, because it does not look like a failure. MSTest's discoverer enumerates types carrying `[TestClass]` and only then looks at their methods; a class without the attribute is never opened, so every `[TestMethod]` in it is silently skipped. Nothing is reported as ignored, no runner prints a warning, and the count of executed tests simply does not include them — a suite that was never run and a suite that passed are the same colour. The signal is decidable from attributes alone, which is what separates it from `SK8001`: no call has to be followed and no assertion has to be recognised, so there is no undecidable middle for the rule to guess at.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **MSTest only, deliberately, and the other two frameworks are silence rather than coverage.** xUnit discovers a `[Fact]` in any public class and has no class-level attribute to be missing; NUnit has made `[TestFixture]` optional since NUnit 3 for a non-generic, non-parameterised class, so its absence is not a defect. A rule that fired on those would be reporting a convention, not a bug. The whole analyzer withdraws unless `Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting.TestMethodAttribute` resolves in the compilation, so a repository with no MSTest reference never sees it. ⚠ **The attribute is matched by symbol through its base chain, never by written name**, so `[DataTestMethod]` and a repository's own `[TestMethod]`-derived attribute are both recognised and somebody else's type called `TestMethodAttribute` is not. ⚠ `[TestClass]` is looked for on the *symbol* and on every base type, so a `partial` class carrying it in another file and a base class carrying it for its derived fixtures are both silence. ⚠ **`abstract` and `static` classes never fire.** An abstract class holding `[TestMethod]` members is the shared-base pattern MSTest supports — the attribute belongs on the concrete class that inherits them — and a static class cannot be a test class at all. ⚠ **One finding per type, not per partial part**, anchored at the first declaring reference in file order, because two findings would each carry an insertion of an attribute that `AllowMultiple` forbids twice. ⚠ **The other direction the upstream idea pairs with this one is not implemented and that is a decision, not an omission.** "A public method in a `[TestClass]` has no test attribute" is not decidable from attributes: a public helper, a public fixture property, a public constructor and a `[TestInitialize]` spelled through somebody's own attribute are all legitimate, and the rule would fire on the ordinary shape of every test file. ⚠ **`fixIsSafe` is false, and not because the edit is uncertain.** There is exactly one repair and it is one token. Its *effect* is that tests which have never executed begin executing, and the first run after it is applied may be red — which is the rule finishing its sentence and is still a thing a person reads before pushing.

rules.title: The test class declares no test
rules.summary: A class marked `[TestClass]` or `[TestFixture]` declares no test method, in itself or in any base type, so the runner opens it and reports nothing about it.
rules.rationale: The attribute is a declaration of intent that the file no longer keeps. A fixture that lost its last test to a refactor — renamed away, moved to another class, commented out during a bisect and never restored — still looks exactly like a fixture that passes, because a class with nothing to run produces no output of any kind. It is `SK8020`'s silence approached from the other side, and like `SK8020` it is decided from attributes alone: the question is whether any method on the type or on a base type carries a test attribute, and answering it follows no call. That is what keeps it out of the territory `SK8001` was cut for.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **MSTest and NUnit only, and xUnit's absence is a decision.** xUnit has no class-level attribute, so there is no declaration of intent for an empty class to contradict; covering it would mean deciding from the class's *name* that it was meant to hold tests, which is a convention rather than a fact and is the guess this rule exists not to make. ⚠ **Inherited tests are tests.** The search walks the whole base chain, including base types that live in another assembly, so the common shared-fixture shape — an annotated base holding the cases and a derived class parameterising them — is silence. ⚠ **A lifecycle hook makes the attribute meaningful and stops the rule.** MSTest requires `[TestClass]` on the type holding `[AssemblyInitialize]` or `[AssemblyCleanup]`, so a hooks-only class is correct code that this rule must not report; `[ClassInitialize]`, `[ClassCleanup]`, `[TestInitialize]`, `[TestCleanup]` and NUnit's `[SetUp]`, `[TearDown]`, `[OneTimeSetUp]` and `[OneTimeTearDown]` are treated the same way. ⚠ **`abstract` never fires**, which is the escape hatch for the shared-base pattern and also for the residual case this rule does not decide: a *concrete* annotated base class that exists only for its derived fixtures to extend will be reported, and marking it `abstract` — which it almost always should be — is both the suppression and the repair. ⚠ **One finding per type, not per partial part.** ⚠ **`hasFix: false`, and there is no version of this that has one.** The two repairs are to write the test the file is missing and to delete the class, and choosing between them is the entire content of the finding; an edit that picked one would be the tool deciding whether a piece of test coverage was meant to exist.

rules.title: The assertion's expected and actual arguments are swapped
rules.summary: An equality assertion is called as `(actual, expected)`: the `expected` argument is not a constant and the `actual` argument is, so the failure message names the two the wrong way round.
rules.rationale: The test passes and fails on exactly the same inputs; what is wrong is the diagnosis. `Assert.Equal(count, 3)` fails with "Expected: 0, Actual: 3" when `count` is 0 — which says the code produced 3 and the author wanted 0, the precise opposite of what happened. Every reading of that failure starts from a reversed diff, and the reader who trusts it goes looking for the bug in the wrong half of the program. The signal is one asymmetry and it needs no guess about intent: a constant cannot be produced by the code under test, so a constant in the `actual` position is the wrong way round.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Evidence in one direction only.** The rule fires when the `expected` argument has no constant value and the `actual` argument has one. Both constant, or neither, is silence — there is nothing to distinguish the two and picking one would be a rewrite of somebody's test rather than a repair of it. ⚠ **xUnit, MSTest and NUnit, matched by parameter name rather than by a list of signatures.** The method must have exactly two parameters called `expected` and `actual`, in that order, on `Xunit.Assert`, `Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting.Assert`, `NUnit.Framework.Assert` or `NUnit.Framework.Legacy.ClassicAssert`. That is what covers `Equal`, `NotEqual`, `StrictEqual`, `Same`, `AreEqual`, `AreNotEqual` and `AreSame` without naming any of them, and it is also what excludes NUnit's constraint form — `Assert.That(actual, Is.EqualTo(expected))` is the opposite order and correct, and its parameters are not called this. A repository's own `Assert` class is not matched at all. ⚠ **Both parameters must have the same type, and that is what makes the fix safe rather than merely plausible.** Overload resolution and generic inference over two arguments of one parameter type are symmetric, so the reversed call binds to the same method with the same type arguments. Where the two types differ the reversed call can bind elsewhere or fail to infer — which is the failure docs/plan/08 records for `SK8002`, where `Assert.NotEqual(0, flags & Member)` does not compile because the `0` was an implicit constant conversion that the rewrite drops. ⚠ **A named argument is silence.** `Assert.Equal(actual: x, expected: 3)` states the order explicitly and is not wrong; swapping the positions would change what it means. ⚠ Reordering is unobservable as well as type-safe: the argument being moved is a constant, so it has no side effect and evaluation order cannot matter. ⚠ **A third argument stops the rule**, including a comparer or a precision, because the method then has three parameters and does not match.

rules.title: The documentation duplicates the base member's
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_inheritdoc_consider_usage_highlighting = none` and this rule defaults to `suggestion`. Reading the ReSharper key — off by default, doc 03 § "Severities" — switches it off. The difference is deliberate rather than an oversight: this rule fires only where the two comments are *identical*, which ReSharper's inspection does not require, so the finding it produces is narrower and does not need the low severity that keeps the wider one usable. docs/plan/16 § Q5.
rules.summary: A member's documentation comment is word for word the one on the member it overrides or implements, so `<inheritdoc />` says the same thing and cannot fall out of step with it.
rules.rationale: A copied doc comment is accurate on the day it is written and has no mechanism keeping it so. The base member's prose is the one a reader treats as authoritative, and when it is edited the copy below silently starts describing the previous behaviour — which is worse than no documentation, because a reader has no way to tell which of the two is stale. `<inheritdoc />` cannot drift, because there is nothing for it to drift from: it is a reference rather than a copy, and it is exactly as long as the claim it makes.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Identical, not similar, and there is deliberately no threshold.** The two comments are compared as their text with the `///` markers stripped and runs of whitespace collapsed, ordinally. A word changed, an `<exception>` added, a `<param>` the base does not carry — any of those is prose saying something the base does not, and replacing it with `<inheritdoc />` would delete it. A similarity score is what would make this rule dangerous, so it does not have one. ⚠ **Three ways to have a base member, all covered, and ambiguity is silence.** An `override`, an explicit interface implementation and an implicit one all resolve; a member that implements *two* interface members resolves to nothing, because `<inheritdoc />` would have to pick one and picking is not a mechanical edit. ⚠ **A member documented in more than one block is left alone**, because the fix replaces a span and an ordinary comment sitting between two documentation blocks would be deleted with them. ⚠ **A base in metadata is compared through its XML documentation file**, and a referenced assembly shipped without one answers with nothing — which is silence, not a match. ⚠ **The one real behaviour change is downstream of the compiler.** `csc` writes `<inheritdoc />` into the generated XML documentation file literally rather than expanding it, so a consumer that reads that file without resolving inheritdoc sees a member with no prose. Every current documentation generator and the IDE do resolve it; a bespoke XML post-processor may not, and that is the case to check before turning this on. It is why the rule ships at `suggestion` rather than `warning`.

rules.title: A non-public member has no documentation comment
rules.summary: A declaration that is not publicly visible through its whole containing chain, and carries no documentation comment. Disabled by default; enable it per path.
rules.rationale: `SK7010` is this rule over the public surface, and the two are meant to partition one population: the same predicates decide what a documentable declaration is, and the only difference is which side of the accessibility line it falls on. What is different is the volume. This is the highest-firing uncovered inspection in the whole parity measurement — 3 408 findings — and `SK7010`, which already ships, produces 1 868 on `Testing/corpus` at `warning`. So it ships **disabled**: `defaultSeverity: none`, the same as `SK7010`, turned on per path by a repository that wants it for the code where internal documentation earns its keep. That is a decision about a report, not about a rule: a finding nobody can see past is not a finding.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Disabled by default, so it produces nothing until a repository asks for it, and that is the whole disposal of its noise.** docs/plan/17 names this the clearest case in the parity map for not letting a fire count drive a decision, and the count is why it ships at `none` rather than why it ships loud. Turning it on repository-wide on a codebase that has never documented an internal is the failure docs/plan/16 § R3 describes; the intended use is a scoped `.editorconfig` section over the paths where it means something. ⚠ **Its predicates are `SK7010`'s, unchanged, with the accessibility test negated**, and that is deliberate rather than convenient: the two rules are meant to partition one population, so a declaration cannot be reported by both or missed by both because they disagree about what is documentable. It therefore inherits every one of `SK7010`'s exclusions — accessors, explicit interface implementations, operators, finalizers, `record` positional members and generated code are not reported, an `<inheritdoc/>` counts as documentation, and an empty `///` does not. ⚠ **Fields are excluded, and for a non-public rule that is the largest single exclusion there is.** Private fields outnumber every other kind of non-public member and a `count` field's name is its documentation; including them is how the rule would become unusable even for the repositories that want it. ⚠ **An `override` is reported**, for the same reason `SK7010` reports one: this rule asks whether the declaration is documented, and `SK7100` is the rule that says what to write there. ⚠ Because it is disabled by default, Roslyn does not run this analyzer at all in a repository that has not enabled it — which is why it is a separate analyzer rather than a branch of the metrics pass, where the predicate would run on every member of every compilation.
configuration: dotnet_diagnostic.SK7101.severity (`none` by default; set it per path to enable)

rules.title: The control flow does nothing
rules.summary: A jump, a `default:` section or a `catch` that transfers control to where control was already going.
rules.rationale: ⚠ **`catch (X) { throw; }` is the member that matters and the other two are housekeeping beside it.** A rethrowing catch reads as error handling: it is where a reader goes looking for the recovery, the wrapping, the logging — and there is none. `throw;` preserves the stack trace, so unlike `SK2015`'s `throw ex;` there is not even a defect underneath it; the clause is inert, and every question it raises has the answer "nothing happens here", which is what the code would say with no `catch` at all. The other two shapes are the same sentence about ordinary control flow: a `continue;` at the end of a loop body jumps to the next iteration that was one statement away, a `return;` at the end of a void body leaves a method that was about to end, and a `default:` section that only breaks describes what a `switch` with no matching section already does.

examples.good: Write(path, payload);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Only the last `catch` of a `try` is ever reported, and that is correctness rather than caution.** Deleting an earlier one changes which handler an exception reaches: in `try { … } catch (IOException) { throw; } catch (Exception e) { Log(e); }` the first clause is what stops an `IOException` being logged, so removing it is a behaviour change wearing a redundancy's clothes. Removing the *last* clause can only leave the exception propagating, which is what the rethrow already did. A `catch` carrying a `when` filter is never reported: the filter runs code, and a filter that returns false leaves the exception to a later clause. ⚠ **Where the rethrowing `catch` is the only one and there is no `finally`, the fix has to replace the whole `try` by its block's contents** — `try { … }` alone is CS1524 — and that is offered only when the block declares nothing, because unwrapping a scope moves every local, local function and label it holds into the enclosing scope where a name that was never in conflict can now collide. A try block that declares a local is left alone rather than fixed badly, and so the finding is withheld. The same is true when the `try` is an embedded statement rather than a statement in a block, because the splice would have more than one statement and nowhere to put it. ⚠ **`goto default;` anywhere in the switch withdraws the `default:` finding**, because the section is the jump's target and deleting it turns a redundancy into CS0159. A `default:` sharing its section with a `case` label is a different shape and is not matched. ⚠ **The `return;` half reads the written return type and never a symbol**, so it matches the `void` keyword, constructors, destructors and `set`/`init`/`add`/`remove` accessors. `async Task` is the same redundancy and is deliberately not matched: `Task` is a name that can be aliased, and answering it needs a semantic model this rule does not ask for. ⚠ **There is no iterator guard, and the belief that one was needed is refuted.** A bare `return;` inside an iterator is not legal C# and does not mean `yield break`: the compiler rejects it with CS1622. The guard was written, committed with a negative fixture, and the fixture failed to compile — an iterator cannot contain the shape this rule matches, so nothing has to exclude it. ⚠ **A comment or a preprocessor directive inside the span withdraws the finding.** The fix deletes the span, `default: break; // nothing to do for the rest` is the author answering the question the reader was about to ask, and a cleanup that silently deletes prose has made the file worse than it found it. ⚠ The boolean-expression members of this family — `RedundantBoolCompare`, `DoubleNegationOperator`, `NegativeEqualityExpression`, `RedundantTernaryExpression`, `RedundantLogicalConditionalExpressionOperand` — are **not** covered. Each needs to know an operand's type before it is redundant rather than meaningful (`x == true` is not redundant for a `bool?`, and `!` may be overloaded), which would make this rule semantic and stop it running on a loose file. `RedundantIfElseBlock`, `RedundantCaseLabel` and `RedundantEnumCaseLabelForDefaultSection` are not covered either.

rules.title: The modifier has no effect
rules.summary: A keyword that restates what the enclosing declaration has already said: `abstract` on an interface member, `sealed` inside a `sealed` type, `class` after `record`, `: int` on an enum, `readonly` inside a `readonly struct`.
rules.rationale: A modifier that does nothing is worse than noise, because a reader cannot tell it from one that does. `sealed` on a member of a `sealed` class invites the question of which derived type was going to override it, and there is none; `abstract` on an interface member suggests the interface has members that are not; `readonly` on one member of a `readonly struct` suggests the others are mutable. Each one is answered by a keyword written a few lines above it, and deleting it makes the declaration say exactly what it meant.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`static` withdraws the interface half entirely, and getting it wrong would have been this rule's worst false positive.** A static interface member is *not* implicitly abstract: C# 11's `static abstract T operator +(T, T)` is an abstract static member, and the same declaration without the keyword is a static member that must have a body. Deleting `abstract` there does not tidy anything — it produces a declaration that no longer compiles. ⚠ **A nested type is never the subject.** A type declared inside an interface is not implicitly abstract, and a type nested in a `sealed` class is not implicitly sealed, so the modifier there is the author's; no type declaration is registered as a candidate. ⚠ **A field inside a `readonly struct` is excluded and that is not an oversight.** CS8340 requires every instance field of one to be `readonly`, so the keyword is the language's rather than the author's and deleting it is an error. ⚠ **`enum E : Int32` is left alone.** The rule matches the `int` keyword only, because it has no semantic model to ask what an identifier resolves to and `Int32` is an ordinary identifier that a using directive or a user type can point somewhere else; the keyword cannot be aliased or shadowed, which is what makes matching it exact. ⚠ **A comment or a directive in the keyword's trailing trivia withdraws the finding.** The fix deletes from the keyword to the next token so that a leading documentation comment and attribute list survive, and that span carries the trailing trivia with it — `public /* still virtual in the base */ sealed override` would lose the note under a fix marked safe. ⚠ Six of [#129](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/129)'s eleven inspections are **not** covered. `PartialTypeWithSinglePart` and `PartialMethodWithSinglePart` are the high-volume pair and both need to count a symbol's declarations across the whole compilation — which a source generator can add to after the fact, so a repository whose generated part is missing from a loose load would be told to delete a `partial` it needs. `RedundantVirtualModifier`, `RedundantScopedParameterModifier`, `RedundantUnsafeContext` and `RedundantOverflowCheckingContext` each need to know something about a body or a type that is not written in the declaration.

rules.title: The `#nullable` directive changes nothing
rules.summary: A `#nullable` directive that sets the annotation and warning state the file is already in.
rules.rationale: `#nullable` directives accumulate during a migration and then stay, at which point they silently override the project-level setting for a file nobody remembers exempting. The state they move is two independent settings — annotations and warnings — each of which is enabled, disabled, or inherited from the project, so a directive is redundant exactly when it moves neither. Deleting one that moves neither is the whole of the edit: the file's nullable state before it and after it are the same state.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The file's opening state is *inherited*, not enabled, which is what makes this rule exact without a project.** The first `#nullable enable` in a file is never reported: whether the project already enables annotations is not written in the file, and this rule does not guess at it. What the opening state does settle is the other direction — a `#nullable restore` before any other directive restores the project default the file already had, and that is a no-op under every project setting there is. ⚠ **A conditional directive anywhere in the file withdraws every finding in it.** Which `#nullable` directives are live inside `#if` depends on the preprocessor symbols the compilation was given, so a file that is clean under one `#define` set and redundant under another has no single answer, and a fix applied under the wrong one deletes a directive the other configuration needs. An *inactive* directive is likewise never read as moving the state, because it does not. ⚠ **A comment on the directive withdraws the finding**, because the fix deletes the whole line and `#nullable disable // the generated half is not annotated yet` is the author explaining a migration — a directive that is redundant today is exactly the kind whose note says why it is there. ⚠ **The four constraint inspections in [#135](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/135) are not covered**: `RedundantNotNullConstraint`, `RedundantNullableAnnotationOnReferenceTypeConstraint`, `RedundantNullableAnnotationOnTypeConstraintHasNonNullableBaseType` and `RedundantNullableAnnotationOnTypeConstraintHasNonNullableTypeKind` each need to know what a constraint's type argument is before the annotation on it can be called redundant, which is a semantic question and a different rule. Nor is the comparison against the project's own `NullableContextOptions`, which is the other half of `UnusedNullableDirective`: in `--load=loose` that value is whatever the loader chose rather than what the project says, so reading it would make the rule report a different set of findings depending on how the file was loaded.

rules.title: The qualifier is redundant
rules.summary: A namespace- or type-qualified type name the simple name already binds to, or a `base.` that reaches the same member as no qualifier.
rules.rationale: A qualifier is how a reader is told that the short name would have meant something else, so one that changes nothing is a false signal: `System.Text.StringBuilder` beside a `using System.Text;` says there is an ambiguity to resolve, and there is not. `base.` says louder still — it says the containing type has its own member of that name and this call deliberately goes past it. `SK0207` owns the `this.` qualifier and `SK0215` the static one; these are the two shapes the arrangement rules leave.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Neither half is decided by comparing text.** The type half asks the semantic model to bind the short name *at the same position* and reports only when it produces the same symbol with no candidates, which is what makes a shadowing type, a missing using directive and a genuine ambiguity each answer for themselves. Deciding it by looking for a matching using directive would be a different rule, and it would be wrong every time two imported namespaces offer the same name. ⚠ **The `base.` half is not "the containing type does not override it", and believing that is how this rule would report a behaviour change as a redundancy.** Given `class A { public virtual void M() { } }`, a `class B : A` calling `base.M()`, and a `class C : B` that overrides `M` — dropping the qualifier in `B` turns a non-virtual call to `A.M` into a virtual one that reaches `C.M`. So the member must be one nothing can override further (not virtual, not abstract, not an unsealed override) or the containing type must be `sealed`. Two further conditions: the containing type must declare nothing of that name, and nothing in scope at that position may be a local, a parameter or a local function of that name, because an unqualified use would find it first. ⚠ **An attribute name is left out.** `[System.Obsolete]` binds to a *constructor* rather than to a type, so the symbol comparison the rest of the rule performs would be comparing the wrong things; the shape is real and it is declined rather than answered with a check that does not mean what it says. ⚠ `global::` is a deliberate disambiguator and is never removed — a short name that binds to the same symbol today is exactly what somebody wrote `global::` to stop depending on. A qualified name inside another one's type arguments is skipped too, because the outer finding and the inner one would be two overlapping edits, and two overlapping edits are not a fix. Using directives, namespace declarations and documentation `cref`s are all positions where the written name *is* the meaning. ⚠ **`UnusedImportClause` belongs to `SK0210`, not here**, and so does `RedundantUsingDirective.Global` — see the note against `SK0210` in docs/plan/08: its removal set is Roslyn's CS8019, and the global-duplication shape reports CS8933, which that filter does not read. Shipping it here would have been a second rule for one concept.

rules.title: The declaration adds nothing
rules.summary: An empty finalizer, an empty sole constructor, an empty namespace, a `: base()` with no arguments, a member initialized to the value it already has, or an `override` that only calls the base.
rules.rationale: ⚠ **The empty finalizer is not merely redundant, and it stays in this rule at `warning` rather than moving to the performance range.** An empty `~Foo() { }` opts the type into finalization: every instance goes on the finalizer queue, survives the collection that would otherwise have taken it, and is freed a generation later — for a body that does nothing. It is kept here because the finding and the edit are the same as the other five, a declaration that adds nothing being deleted; splitting it out would have made one concept two ids for the sake of a severity, and the cost is instead in the message, where a reader will actually see it. The other five are deletions with no effect at all: the compiler generates exactly the constructor that was written, supplies exactly that constructor initializer, zero-initializes exactly that field, and dispatches to exactly the base method the override forwards to.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **A `static` constructor is never this shape and an empty one is not redundant.** Declaring one — even empty — clears `beforefieldinit` on the type, which changes when the runtime is allowed to run the type's initialization; deleting it is a timing change and not a cleanup. ⚠ The constructor shape is classes only, never a `partial` one and never one with a primary constructor: in a partial type the other part may hold the constructor that makes this one meaningful, and it is not visible from here. It must also be the only instance constructor, and its accessibility must be the one the compiler would have generated — `protected` on an abstract class and `public` on every other — because an accessibility that differs is doing something. ⚠ **`= null` is accepted only on a type written with a `?`, and `= default` on the same set plus the value-type keywords.** Under an enabled nullable context `string name = null;` warns at the initializer (CS8625), and deleting it moves the warning to CS8618 at the constructor — a *different* warning, which a fix marked safe may not introduce. `string`, `object` and every user-written type are therefore out, because whether one is a struct is not visible in the declaration. `0f`, `0m` and `'\0'` are the same value written differently and are not matched; an enum member and a struct's own `Empty` are not decidable here at all. Automatically implemented properties only — an accessor with a body stores wherever its code says. ⚠ **The `override` shape is `void`-only, and that is the covariant-return guard.** C# 9 lets an override narrow its return type, and such an override is the declaration carrying the narrower type, so deleting it changes what every caller sees; comparing the two return types needs the base symbol, which this rule does not ask for, so the question is excluded by matching the `void` keyword instead. `sealed`, an attribute, a type parameter list and a parameter with a default value each withdraw it as well. ⚠ **The fix deletes a declaration's *full* span, which begins at its leading trivia**, so a documentation comment, an ordinary comment, a `#region` or an attribute list withdraws the finding rather than being carried away by a fix marked safe. ⚠ Eight of [#130](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/130)'s fourteen inspections are not covered. `RedundantTypeDeclarationBody` is the notable one and it is **declined rather than pending**: it asks for `class Foo { }` to become `class Foo;`, and `SK6023` reports the same braces as an unfinished declaration — two rules would disagree about one span. `RedundantExtendsListEntry`, `RedundantAttributeSuffix` and `RedundantExplicitPositionalPropertyDeclaration` each need a symbol; `RedundantPartialMethodEmptyImplementation` needs the other part; `RedundantSetterValueParameterDeclaration`, `RedundantSetsRequiredMembersAttribute` and `RedundantAttributeUsageProperty` are each a distinct edit that this rule does not attempt.

rules.title: Use pattern matching instead of a test-and-cast
rules.summary: A conversion followed by a null check, a safe cast used only as a type test, or a negated type check is a pattern.
rules.rationale: `var b = x as Binary; if (b != null)` converts, stores, and then asks whether the conversion worked — three steps for one question the language has had an answer to since C# 7. `x is Binary b` is one `isinst`, one variable, and a relationship the reader does not have to reconstruct from two adjacent statements. The same holds for `(x as T) != null`, which allocates a conversion result nobody wants in order to test a type, and for `!(x is T)`, which reads as the negation of a question rather than as the question the code is actually asking.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`SK1015` owns `is T` followed by a cast; this rule is the rest of the family and never restates it.** Four shapes: an `as` conversion whose very next statement is an `if` testing it for null, a safe cast compared against null (`(x as T) != null` → `x is T`), a negated type test (`!(x is T)` → `x is not T`), and a type check that succeeds for every non-null value of the operand's own static type (`s is object` → `s is not null`). ⚠ The `as`-plus-null-check shape requires **every** reference to the local to be inside the `if` it guards: a pattern variable is not definitely assigned after the `if`, so a use below it would be CS0165, and an `else` branch is refused for the same reason. The conversion operand must be a chain of plain names, so nothing that could be evaluated for a side effect moves into a condition. ⚠ The tested type must be a reference type — `x is int?` is CS8116 — and a null comparison whose operand type declares `operator ==` is left alone, because `==` there is not the reference test the pattern makes. ⚠ The two shapes that produce a `not` pattern are silent below C# 9 even though the rule's floor is C# 7, and every shape is silent inside an expression tree, where a pattern is CS8122, and where rewriting would change what the tree contains. ⚠ **Not covered, and deliberately so:** `UseSwitchCasePatternVariable` (a `switch` case that casts in its body), `ConvertTypeCheckPatternToNullCheck`, and the negated `as` guard (`if (t == null) return;`), which needs a reachability proof the other shapes do not.

rules.title: Simplify the pattern
rules.summary: A run of `not` that cancels itself, or a `not` in front of a relational pattern that the operator already spells.
rules.rationale: Patterns compose, so they also accumulate. `SK1011` and `SK1014` introduce property and relational patterns and nothing tidies them afterwards, which is how a modernization rule creates its own debt: a `not` added to an existing `not` during a refactor, or a `not (> 5)` written because the condition it replaced was `!(x > 5)`. Neither survives being read aloud, and both have an exact spelling that does.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`not (> 5)` is `<= 5` only where the type's order is total, which is why this rule is `Semantic` rather than the `Syntax` its proposal assumed.** On `double`, `NaN > 5` is false, so `not (> 5)` matches `NaN` and `<= 5` does not; on `int?`, `not (> 5)` matches `null` and `<= 5` does not. Both rewrites look like De Morgan's law and neither is one, so the inversion is admitted only for a non-nullable `sbyte`/`byte`/`short`/`ushort`/`int`/`uint`/`long`/`ulong`/`char`/`decimal`/`nint`/`nuint` or an enum, and the input type is read from the `is` operand or the governing expression of the `switch` — a `not` inside a property subpattern or a list pattern is declined because the walk cannot see what it is being matched against. ⚠ Cancelling a run of `not` is unconditional and needs none of that; only the relational inversion does. ⚠ **The top of a `not` run owns the finding**, so a triple negation is one rewrite rather than two overlapping ones, and an odd residual is folded into the inversion instead of being left for a second pass — a rule that still fires after its own fix turns `skala fix` into a loop. ⚠ **The residual pattern keeps whatever parentheses it had**: `not` binds tighter than `and`, so unwrapping `Z and not not (A or B)` would produce `Z and A or B`, a different predicate. ⚠ Not covered: `RedundantIsBeforeRelationalPattern`, `ReplaceObjectPatternWithVarPattern`, `ExtractCommonPropertyPattern` and `ReplaceSequenceEqualWithConstantPattern`, each of which is a different rewrite with its own proof obligation.

rules.title: Merge the `?:` into a conditional access
rules.summary: A conditional whose only job is to guard a member access against null is a `?.`.
rules.rationale: `x != null ? x.Y : null` names the receiver three times to say one thing, and the thing it says is what `?.` was added to the language for. The rewrite also reads the receiver once instead of twice, which is the point at which it stops being cosmetic: two reads of the same path is a shape where a reader has to check that nothing changed in between, and the conditional access removes the question.

examples.bad: return document != null ? document.Root : null;
examples.good: return document?.Root;
